article_text:
As Julia Stiles paid tribute to Heath Ledger on Dancing with the Stars , one 10 Things I Hate About You star was unable to attend the televised reunion.

Following Tuesday’s “Dedication Night” on Season 35 of the ABC dance competition show, David Krumholtz explained why he was not able to join his co-stars in supporting Stiles at the live taping.

“Good morning, here I am in the Catskill Mountains, upstate New York. Fall foliage in full effect,” he began in a video on Instagram. “I am here shooting a film. I could not be in LA for Dancing with the Stars last night.”

‘Dancing With The Stars’ Season 35 Cast: All The Celebrities Vying For Mirrorball Trophy In ABC Competition

Krumholtz continued, “I would have loved, loved, loved to have been there. Everyone looked so amazing. Julia’s tribute to my dear friend who I miss every single day was amazing and stunning, and I’m so proud of her. And I thought the cast looked amazing.

Watch on Deadline

“They all look so young still, and it would have been weird,” said Krumholtz, taking off his beanie to reveal a bald spot. “Because I shaved what’s left of my hair, and then it becomes a whole internet fodder. ‘Oh, look what happened to him.’ I didn’t want that. But that’s not why I wasn’t there. I would have dealt with it. Anyway, love them all, love you all.”

View this post on Instagram

Stiles commented on Krumholtz’s post, “We love you Krumholtz!”

After Stiles performed a dance with pro Ezra Sosa to Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You”, she was joined onstage by her 10 Things co-stars Larisa Oleynik, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Gabrielle Union, Andrew Keegan and Susan May Pratt.

Following the performance, Stiles noted in an interview with ET that Krumholtz “wanted to be here but he’s working on an HBO show in New York, so there was no way he could fly to Los Angeles.” She appears to be referring to Matthew Barry’s true-crime limited series The Trial of Louise Woodward .

Krumholtz’s post comes after he explained in August that he recently “ decided to put my career on hold ” to focus on his mental health, following a previous announcement that some believed was him retiring.

title_original: The Social Reckoning isn’t as angry or as potent as a Facebook drama should be
editorial_title_zh: 《The Social Reckoning》既不够愤怒，也不具备一部 Facebook 电影应有的震撼力
editorial_excerpt_zh: 阿伦·索尔金（Aaron Sorkin）试图重现《社交网络》的成功，却对一个需要更敏锐目光的世界给出了一部出奇过时且不完整的审视。回过头来看，大卫·芬奇（David Fincher）2010 年的电影《社交网络》是一个具有里程碑意义的作品，其原因静水深流，甚至有点反直觉。在……

Facebook 起源故事的合适人选。虽然索尔金或许把马克·扎克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）转换成了他能更好理解的设定——即一个语速极快、内心深处其实是想给聪明严肃的女孩留下深刻印象的自作聪明者——但他与芬奇也将这部电影打造成了最早以互联网为中心的电影之一，它将线上生活视为现实生活中动态的自然延伸，而不是像许多 90 年代互联网电影那样将其描绘为超现实的技术门户。", "links": Children）就因采取了一种惊恐主义的方法——将互联网视为寻求婚外情的成年人、滋生色情成瘾的青少年以及各年龄段渴望出名的攀附者的避难所——而遭到广泛嘲讽。相比之下，《社交网络》对 Facebook 的基本运作机制表现得极为不带偏见，它将初露端倪的缺陷根植于孕育它的那些人性弱点之中。回想起来，这部电影只有在它低估了扎克伯格对权力的攫取以及他的线上王国所建立于其上的严峻粗心大意时，才会让人觉得过时。", "links": [{"text": "Facebook", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/facebook"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《The Social Reckoning》是一部由索尔金编剧并执导、但芬奇并未参与其中的类续集作品，它旨在纠正历史记录，同时仍为一个坚信该网站具有真正实用性的角色发声。弗朗西丝·豪根（Frances 正在助长部分用户的激进化、作为其言论自由“给人民想要的东西”这一运作方式的副产品将他们引入极端主义群体时，她感到痛心疾首。她转向了一位正在挖掘该公司内幕的、带有勒德分子色彩的记者（杰瑞米·艾伦·怀特饰），两人联手挑战了扎克伯格的绝对权威——在《社交网络》的结尾，扎克伯格曾无果地刷新着 Facebook 页面，期盼着能收到一个互加好友的请求。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一部背景大体设定在 2020 年代初期的电影，《The Social Reckoning》里的扎克伯格完全换了个人，字面意义上的：以极度紧绷著称的杰瑞米·斯特朗（Jeremy Strong）接替了相对迷人的杰西·艾森伯格（Jesse Eisenberg）。但扎克尽管在这里也不是绝对的焦点；虽然他被描绘成第一部电影中那个受委屈的书呆子的某种变体，依然吐出尖锐讽刺的言辞，却带有一种空心西装自动化身般的声腔，这部电影想要探讨的是社交网络如何已经扩散到失控于扎克伯格的程度。他无法对现实生活中的不良影响做任何事情——他抱怨无论自己做什么都将面临两面不讨好的攻击——所以他索性让利润继续滚滚而来。", "links": [{"text": {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，索尔金也坚持用陈腐、老派的词汇来限定这种行为。1 月 6 日的暴动被定性为大体上极其出格，在很大程度上是因为它们给警务人员造成了伤害——这与电影的开场序列相呼应，其中一个喝醉且种族主义的女性在 Facebook 上向非白人警察直播了她可怕的评论。难道就没人想想警察吗？！（这仿佛是索尔金无法想象如此赤裸的种族主义，除非它得到了警方官方记录的背书。）这就是索尔金察觉到适当秩序受到威胁的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": 的职务并在国会作证时，电影借她的高光时刻暗示清算即将来临，扎克伯格在某种程度上已经受到了惩戒和/或羞辱。世界已被拉回悬崖边缘。与此同时，针对 Facebook 甚至更有罪凿的指控——比如该公司在缅甸促成了种族灭绝这一说法——却连提都没提。人们不能指望一部电影涵盖全球互联网的全部，但这并未能阻止《The Social Reckoning》让人感觉异常狭隘。", "links": [{"text": "另一个更含蓄的迹象表明，索金并没有真正融入现实的2020年代，而是更偏爱一个已经不复存在的世界：他在整部电影中调用的每一个文化参考点，都可以追溯到大约20世纪中期。这位记者热爱《演艺船》。随后，他对弗朗西斯提及弗兰克·卡普拉感到惊喜和欣慰，接着便推荐了这位导演更多的电影，因为她只看过其中两部。扎克伯格的一位幕僚引用了《吉利根岛》来阐述公众易受骗的观点。除了无法避开的时事外，他最现代的致意也不过是提及伍德沃德和伯恩斯坦。可曾有过这样一部电影，既描绘了Covid-19大流行，又拒绝承认任何不足半个世纪之久流行文化的？", "毫无疑问，他会认为这是一种个人癖好；索金热爱音乐剧，对经典时期的电视节目记忆犹新，他的角色亦当如此。他无意中创造的是一个几乎与早期互联网奇幻片（如《黑客帝国》或《杀手网》）一样闭塞且不切实际的世界，在这个世界里，卡普拉式的胜利依然触手可及。索金明白互联网是现实生活的一部分，而不是一种神秘的时尚，亦非一个纯粹的赛博世界。他并没有像他的一些反对者在2010年所担忧的那样“愤怒对抗机器”。但他对现实生活本身的构想，却似乎停留在这样一个时代：即使不是史前互联网时代，至少也是前特朗普时代。1月6日对那个Facebook控制室来说或许是一个令人清醒的事件，但在这样一个世界里，所有人都得到了赦免，那个利用社交媒体煽动暴乱的总统再度当选并变得更加有恃无恐。也许，历经这么多年之后，电影中那些对互联网更为危言耸听的看法并非那么离谱。与《艾丁顿》的兔子洞、《红房间》的狂乱心理，甚至是大卫·柯南伯格的《裹尸布》中那些被媒介化的世界相比，《社交清算》对互联网电影的审视似乎还不够偏执、不够愤怒，也不够惊恐。索金可能以为自己正用雪亮的双眼审视互联网，但他其实戴着眼罩。", article_text:
I n retrospect, David Fincher’s 2010 film The Social Network was a landmark for a quiet, even counterintuitive reason. Before the film was released, some questioned whether Aaron Sorkin, a writer not exactly known for his mastery of, nevermind obsession with, the technical sphere, was the right man to tell the origin story of Facebook. And while Sorkin may well have converted Mark Zuckerberg into terms he could better understand – namely, a motormouthed wiseass who deep down wants to impress a smart, serious-minded girl – he and Fincher also made one of the first internet-centric movies to treat online life as a natural extension of IRL dynamics, rather than the otherworldly tech portal seen in so many 90s internet movies.

Granted, that’s the whole deal with Facebook: its viral spread of social networking, something so simple and addictive that aunts, grandpas and co-workers everywhere could understand it. Yet understanding its simultaneous extension and distortion of the real world wasn’t a given; four years later, for example, 2014’s Men, Women and Children was widely derided for taking an alarmist approach to the internet as a haven for adults seeking an affair, teenagers nursing porn addictions and fame-hungry strivers of all ages. The Social Network, on the other hand, is remarkably nonjudgmental about the basic mechanics of Facebook , rooting its nascent flaws in the human weaknesses that birthed it. In retrospect, the movie only feels outdated to the extent that it underestimates Zuckerberg’s grasping for power and the potential for grim carelessness that his online kingdom was built on.

The Social Reckoning, a sorta-sequel written and directed by Sorkin without Fincher’s involvement, aims to correct the record while still giving voice to a character who believes that the site has real utility. Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), who works for the site’s civics team, is socially awkward and anxious, and when she notes that some people are better at a keyboard than they are in person, it’s clear she’s thinking of herself, even though she never says so. Frances is distraught to learn that Facebook is contributing to radicalization of some of its users, funneling them into extremist groups as a function of its give-the-people-what-they-want approach to free speech. She turns to a luddite-adjacent journalist (Jeremy Allen White) doing some digging on the company, and together they challenge the orthodoxy of Zuckerberg, last seen in The Social Network fruitlessly refreshing a Facebook page hoping for a reciprocated friend request.

Appropriate for a movie set largely in the early 2020s, The Social Reckoning’s Zuckerberg is a completely different person, literally: famously intense Jeremy Strong steps in for the comparably charming Jesse Eisenberg. But Zuck isn’t the main focus here anyway; though he is depicted as a sort of mutation of the aggrieved nerd from the first film, still issuing cutting sarcastic remarks, but in the voice of an empty-suit automaton, the movie wants to be about the ways that social networking has metastasized beyond Zuckerberg’s control. He can’t do anything about ill effects on real life – he laments the both-sides attacks he’ll face no matter what he does – so he might as well keep the profits churning in.

It’s here where Sorkin both oversteps and falls short in his analysis of how online reality has bled into the real world. On one hand, he connects the radicalization of some Facebook users to the January 6 insurrection riots in Washington, jumping into the Facebook control room for a chilling look at their inaction in the face of fomenting violence in our own country. Connecting that particular dot requires some timeline fudging of the dual whistleblower-and-Zuckerberg story threads, but you understand why Sorkin went to the trouble. It’s an event representing the kind of behavior that Facebook probably enabled, both ideologically and logistically.

Yet Sorkin also insists on containing that behavior in stodgy, old-fashioned terms. The January 6 riots are framed as particularly far beyond the pale in large part because they bring harm to police officers – which connects back to the movie’s opening sequence, where a drunk and racist woman livestreams her horrible comments to non-white police officers on Facebook. Won’t someone please think of the cops?! (It’s as if Sorkin can’t conceive of racism so blatant unless it’s been officially documented by the police.) This is how Sorkin knows the proper order has been threatened.

When Frances quits her Facebook post and testifies in front of Congress, the movie implies with her moment of triumph that the reckoning is at hand, and that Zuckerberg has been, on some level, chastened and/or humiliated. The world has been pulled back from the brink. Meanwhile, the existence of even more damning cases against Facebook, like the idea that the company enabled genocide in Myanmar , doesn’t get so much as a mention. One movie can’t be expected to cover the whole of the global internet, but that doesn’t stop The Social Reckoning from feeling awfully small.

A more subtle sign that Sorkin hasn’t oriented himself in the actual 2020s, and instead prefers a world that no longer exists: every cultural reference point he summons throughout the movie dates from around the middle of the 20h century. The reporter loves Show Boat. Later, he expresses his surprise and gratification that Frances makes reference to Frank Capra – then proceeds to recommend more of the director’s films, because she’s only seen two of them. A Zuckerberg handler makes reference to Gilligan’s Island to illustrate a point about the public’s gullibility. The most contemporary he gets, apart from the unavoidable current events, is name-checking Woodward and Bernstein. Has there ever been a movie that has somehow both depicted the Covid-19 pandemic and refused to acknowledge popular culture less than a half-century old?

Doubtless he’d consider this a personal quirk; Sorkin loves musical theater and remembers classic-era television, and so shall his characters. What he’s unintentionally done is create a world nearly as insular and fantastical as the ones in early internet fantasies such as Hackers or Virtuosity, one where a Capra-esque triumph remains within arm’s reach of his plucky protagonist. Sorkin gets that the internet is a part of real life, not a mystical fad or a wholly internet world. He’s not raging against the machine, the way some of his detractors feared he might back in 2010. But his conception of real life itself feels stuck in a time that is, if not pre-internet, at very least pre-Trump. January 6 may have been a sobering event in that Facebook control room, but in this world, everyone was pardoned and the president who used social media to egg it was re-elected and further emboldened. Maybe, all these years later, those more alarmist takes on the internet via cinema weren’t so off-base after all. Compared with the rabbit holes of Eddington, the psychosis of Red Rooms, or even the mediated worlds of David Cronenberg’s The Shrouds, The Social Reckoning’s take on the internet movie doesn’t seem nearly paranoid, angry or scared enough. Sorkin may think he’s looking at the internet with clear eyes, but he’s wearing blinders.

article_text:
Such an inspiring tale of the transformative power of cinema ( The one change that worked: numb with grief, I sat in the dark, surrounded by strangers – and began to heal, 12 October ). Having lost my only sister, my father and my wife within a relatively short period, I can attest to the ability of this precious activity to distract, uplift and, well, simply rescue one from the deepest pit of despair. Cinema saves lives – that is absolutely clear to me. Geoffrey Meenan London

I was there at the other Battle of Hastings on 5 March 1966 ( Letters, 12 October ). I was 16 and went with my then boyfriend, who was at Leicester art college. I recall the sack costume and wildly rushing down a hill. That evening I ate spaghetti bolognese (English version) for the first time. My taste for Italian food lasted longer than the boyfriend. Elaine Fear Horsted Keynes, West Sussex

Emma Beddington is looking for autumnal glimmers ( 12 October ). She should join me in our morning bathroom at this time of year, when we have a rainbow on our toilet roll, as the low sun refracts through then reflects from the edge of the mirror opposite. Julia Leach Norwich

My library always sends me a “pre-overdue” notice a few days before the return date for books I’ve borrowed ( Letters, 12 October ). Surely my books are simply due? Lynne Scrimshaw London

Now I feel discriminated against. No one asked me which school I attended when I was at Teesside Polytechnic ( Letters, 11 October ). Keith Langton Kirkcudbright, Dumfries & Galloway

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "美国“硫磺岛纪念碑”遭锤子砸损──士兵雕像头部坠落，嫌疑人被捕", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "位于美国弗吉尼亚州匡提科海军陆战队基地附近的“硫磺岛纪念碑”遭到锤子砸损。警方估计，损失金额相当于数十万美元（数千万日元）。嫌疑人已被捕。", "links": [{"text": "アメリカ", "url": "https://artnewsjapan.com/tag/usa"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://media.artnewsjapan.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/26141723/marines-.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ARTnews JAPAN", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "10月21日晚（当地时间），位于美国东部弗吉尼亚州匡提科海军陆战队基地附近的“硫磺岛纪念碑”遭到锤子砸损。构成士兵雕像的6尊石像中，多尊雕像的头部等部位受损，据警方当局估计，损失金额相当于数十万美元（数千万日元）。", "links": [{"text": "アメリカ", "url": "https://artnewsjapan.com/tag/usa"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "根据案件报告，威廉王子县的警察赶到现场时，嫌疑人米格尔·阿隆索·马尔多纳多·索里亚诺（27岁）据称“正用大锤砸向雕像”。构成纪念碑的士兵雕像中，有1尊的头部脱落，另1尊的头盔和面部“有缺损或刮痕”。此外，还有一尊雕像背负的步枪上的刺刀不见了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因涉嫌破坏财物等罪名被捕的马尔多纳多·索里亚诺是该州斯塔福德的居民。他被指控犯有破坏纪念碑及破坏财物罪（重罪），以及蓄意破坏财物的非法侵入罪（轻罪），但截至本稿撰写时，该嫌疑人的辩护律师尚未发表评论。嫌疑人在等待出庭期间被无保释金羁押。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此次破坏行为中受损的是小型版纪念碑，由曾创作同在弗吉尼亚州阿灵顿的“海军陆战队战争纪念碑”的雕塑家费利克斯·德·韦ルドン操刀。这座纪念碑重现了第二次世界大战末期，硫磺岛摺钵山山顶上6名美军士兵等高举星条旗的姿态。它是根据美联社摄影师乔·罗森塔尔拍摄并荣获普利策奖的照片制作的。", "links": [{"text": "破壊行為", "url": "https://artnewsjapan.com/tag/vandalism"}, {"text": "ピューリッツァー賞", "url": "https://artnewsjapan.com/tag/pulitzerprize"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在太平洋战争末期1945年2月至3月进行的硫磺岛战役中，日美两军展开激战，造成大量人员伤亡。此外，罗森塔尔照片中拍摄的6人里，直到战时结束幸存的有3人，其余3人在硫磺岛战役中丧生。（翻译：石井佳子）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "from ARTnews", "links": [{"text": "ARTnews", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/monument-to-iwo-jima-flag-raising-near-quantico-vandalized-1234803717/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
米「硫黄島記念碑」がハンマーで損壊──兵士像の頭部が落下、容疑者を逮捕

アメリカ ・バージニア州クアンティコ海兵隊基地近くにある「硫黄島記念碑」がハンマーで損壊された。被害額は数十万ドル（数千万円）相当になると警察は推定している。容疑者はすでに逮捕された。

10月21日夜（現地時間）、 アメリカ 東部バージニア州のクアンティコ海兵隊基地近くにある「硫黄島記念碑」が、ハンマーによる損壊の被害を受けた。兵士像を構成する6体の石像のうち、複数の像の頭部などが損傷しており、被害額は数十万ドル（数千万円）相当と警察当局は見ている。

事件の報告書によると、プリンスウィリアム郡の警察官が通報を受けて現場に到着した際、容疑者のミゲル・アロンソ・マルドナド・ソリアーノ（27）が「大型ハンマーを像に振り下ろしていた」とされる。記念碑を構成する兵士像の1体は頭部が落下し、もう1体のヘルメットと顔が「欠けたり、削れたり」していた。また、別の像では、背負った小銃に取り付けられていた銃剣が失われていた。

器物損壊などの疑いで逮捕されたマルドナド・ソリアーノは、同州スタッフォード在住の男性。記念碑損傷および器物損壊（重大犯罪）、ならびに器物損壊の意図を伴う不法侵入（軽犯罪）の容疑で起訴されたが、同容疑者の弁護人側は、本稿執筆時点でコメントを出していない。容疑者は出廷を待つ間、保釈金なしで勾留されている。

今回の 破壊行為 で被害を受けたのは、同じバージニア州のアーリントンにある「海兵隊戦争記念碑」を制作した彫刻家、フェリックス・デ・ウェルドンが手がけた小型版だ。この記念碑は、第2次世界大戦末期、硫黄島の摺鉢山（すりばちやま）山頂で6人の米兵らが星条旗を掲げる姿を再現したもの。AP通信の写真家ジョー・ローゼンタールが撮影し、 ピューリッツァー賞 を受賞した写真をもとに制作された。

太平洋戦争末期の1945年2月から3月にかけて行われた硫黄島の戦いでは、日米両軍が激戦を繰り広げ、多数の死傷者を出した。なお、ローゼンタールの写真に写っている6人のうち終戦まで生き残ったのは3人で、残る3人は、硫黄島の戦いで命を落としている。（翻訳：石井佳子）

article_text:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

Fans won’t have to wait until December to return to Arrakis. Warner Bros. and Legendary Entertainment are bringing the world of Denis Villeneuve’s “ Dune ” films to downtown Los Angeles next month, with a new immersive attraction that lets visitors encounter giant sandworms, sit on Paul Atreides’ throne and get an up-close look at actual props from the blockbuster franchise.

“Dune: The Experience” will open Nov. 20 at 330 S. Alameda St., running through Dec. 20, a month before “Dune: Part Three” arrives in theaters on Dec. 18. The hourlong walkthrough, produced in partnership with entertainment platform Fever , is the latest attempt to turn a major Hollywood property into a ticketed, real-world attraction — and, in this case, capitalize on anticipation for one of the year’s biggest theatrical releases.

Related Stories

'The Big Boom!,' Documentary About Weapons Factory Workers, Picked Up by Lightdox Ahead of IDFA Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)

‘Always Lalisa’ Director Sue Kim Reveals Secrets Behind Lisa Doc, From YG Blocking Blackpink Music to Lots of Tequila Shots

The attraction recreates several of the films’ most recognizable settings, from the desert planet of Arrakis to the imperial throne room. Visitors can take the Bene Gesserit test, decipher hidden Fremen messages and come face-to-face with a colossal sandworm. There’s also a collection of original costumes, weapons, props and production artifacts from across Villeneuve’s trilogy, including a full-scale ornithopter used in the films.

Naturally, there are plenty of photo opportunities. Guests can pose on the Emperor’s throne, recreate moments from the films’ promotional posters and browse a merchandise shop stocked with exclusive collectibles. A themed dining lounge will offer food and drinks inspired by the franchise.

Tickets start at $31.50, with several premium packages available for more committed fans. The $67 deluxe option includes flexible entry, a branded water bottle and a tote bag. At the top end is a $250 package that allows visitors to actually step inside the original ornithopter, along with a digital photo package, a printed keepsake and parking.

“Dune: Part Three,” which Villeneuve directed from a screenplay co-written with Brian K. Vaughan, will conclude his adaptation of Frank Herbert’s science-fiction saga . The new attraction gives Warner Bros. and Legendary another way to keep the franchise in front of audiences during the final stretch of the film’s marketing campaign, while also generating revenue from a property whose appeal now extends well beyond the multiplex.usion of Villeneuve’s trilogy, Warner Bros. and Legendary have a sizable audience to court.

Tickets for “Dune: The Experience” are available through Fever , with the attraction scheduled to run Nov. 20 through Dec. 20 in Los Angeles. Additional cities are expected to be announced.

article_text:
Jane Austen is known for her sharp social commentary and wit embedded in the romance novels she writes. With the newest take on Sense And Sensibility (2026) now out in theaters and another limited series adaptation of Pride and Prejudice on its way to Netflix later this year, many may be wondering what other works of the author have made it to the screen.

Multiple versions of Pride and Prejudice already exist alongside the new redone Sense And Sensibility , and several of the author’s beloved novels have been adapted into film installments or series as well.

RELATED: 10 Of The Best Period Dramas & Where To Stream Them

Find several Jane Austen movies and tv shows below and where to stream them.

‘Sanditon’ (2019-23) Image Credit: PBS Masterpiece Austen’s final and unfinished 1817 novel Sanditon was adapted into a series that aired on ITV in the United Kingdom and then PBS in the United States. Created by Andrew Davies, the series starred Rose Williams as Charlotte Heywood, Crystal Clarke as Georgiana Lambe, Kris Marshall as Tom Parker, Kate Ashfield as Mary Parker, Jack Fox as Sir Edward Denham, Ben Lloyd-Hughes as Alexander Colbourne, Theo James as Sidney Parker and many more. Sanditon can be accessed via Prime Video in addition to PBS in the states.

‘Pride And Prejudice’ (1995) Pride And Prejudice also became a TV miniseries in 1995 starring Colin Firth as Mr. Darcy and Jennifer Ehle as Elizabeth Bennet. Alison Steadman played Mrs. Bennet, and Benjamin Whitrow played Mr. Bennet. The 1995 television series is streaming on Hulu.

‘Pride And Prejudice’ (2005) Image Credit: Focus Features/courtesy Everett collection Keira Knightly led the Joe Wright-directed Pride and Prejudice (2005) as Elizabeth bennet alongside Matthew Macfadyen as Mr. Darcy. Rosamund Pike portrayed Jane Bennet, Jena Malone played Lydia Bennet and Carey Mulligan played Kitty Bennet. Brenda Blethyn played Mrs. Bennet, and the late Donald Sutherland portrayed Mr. Bennet. Simon Woods played Mr. Bingley, Kelley Reilly played Caroline Bingley and Ruper Friend portrayed Mr. Wickham. Who could forget Tom Hollander’s performance as Mr. Collins? The 2005 Pride and Prejudice film is available to rent on Prime Video and Apple TV as well as streaming.

‘Emma’ – 2020 Focus Features was also behind the Autumn de Wilde-directed film adaptation of Emma. (2020). Adapted from Austen’s book by Eleanor Catton, the film starred Anya Taylor-Joy in the titular role of Emma Woodhouse, Johnny Flynn as Mr. Knightley, Mia Goth as Harriet Smith, Bill Nighy as Mr. Woodhouse, Josh O’Connor as Mr. Elton, Connor Swindells as Robert Martin and more. The film is available to rent on Prime Video and Apple TV.

‘Persuasion’ – 2022, Netflix Image Credit: Netflix Dakota Johnson portrayed Anne Elliot in the Netflix film adaptation of Persuasion , which had been done a few times before. The streamer’s version also starred Henry Golding as Mr. Elliot, Cosmo Jarvis as Wentworth and Richard E. Grant as Sir Walter Elliot. The film is streaming on Netflix. The 1995 version is available to rent on Prime Video, Apple TV and streaming on Britbox, the Roku Channel and Tubi as is the 2007 film, which is also streaming on Hulu.

‘Sense And Sensibility’ – 1995 Image Credit: Columbia Pictures / courtesy Everett Collection The Ang Lee-directed film adapted from Sense And Sensibility by Emma Thompson also starred Thompson as Elinor alongside Kate Winslet as Marianne Dashwood. Alan Rickman portrayed Colonel Brandon, and Hugh Grant portrayed Edward Ferrars. The film is not currently streaming anywhere, but it is available to rent on Prime Video and Apple TV.

‘Sense And Sensibility’ – 2026 Image Credit: Focus Features / Courtesy Everett Collection Georgia Oakley’s Sense And Sensibility (2026) is the latest film adaptation to join the collection of Austen novels turned tv and movies. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star in the new version of Austen’s debut novel as the Dashwood sisters, Elinor and Marianne, respectively. Caitríona Balfe portrays Mrs. Dashwood, and Fiona Shaw portrays Mrs. Jennings. The film arrived in theaters October 16.

article_text:
He might be under fire in the U.S., but Ted Sarandos was all smiles in Korea this weekend.

The Netflix co-CEO took to the stage at an event in Seoul marking the streamer’s tenth anniversary in Korea, from where the likes of Squid Game , Kpop Demon Hunters and Kingdom have come. Korea was one of Netflix’s biggest bets financially, and has proven one of its most important markets.

“Ten years ago, we dreamed big, but none of us could have imagined that Korean stories would move hearts around the world, and land right at the center of global culture,” said Sarandos.

Related Stories

'Nobody Wants This' Creator Erin Foster Has "More Story To Tell" With A Season 4, But Isn't Getting "Too Attached"

Quentin Tarantino Wraps His AFI Fest Q&A By Showing Crowd First 17 Minutes Of 'Cliff Booth'

“For Netflix, Korea is more than a market. It is where we discovered new possibilities, and where we learned how far a story can travel, and it is one of our most treasured partners for the future we are building together. To every creator, every actor, every crew member, and every fan in Korea: thank you, from the bottom of my heart.”

Watch on Deadline

Sarandos was speaking after a difficult period for Netflix, during which its shares tumbled despite decent third quarter results. Wall Street remains spooked amid mass layoffs at the streamer and a share price that has fallen sharply throughout 2026.

Netflix countered criticism of its performance in the U.S. by pointing to international titles such as Plastic Beauty , The Secret Woman and The Perfect Lie , which are on track to become the most-watched titles ever in Japan, Denmark and the Netherlands, respectively.

The Korea event will have been a further tonic for Sarandos, with the likes of Lee Jung-lae, Lee Byung-hun and Park Hae-soo from Squid Game , Ahn Hyo-seop from Kpop Demon Hunters and stars from D.P. , Physical 100 , Hellbound , Mask Girl , Culinary Class Wars , The Devil’s Plan and Agent Kim Reactivated taking to stage at the Korea Fan Festival at the Sangnam Oil Tank Culture Park. The event ran October 24 and 25.

Stars from upcoming shows Possible Love , Tantara , Grand Galaxy Hotel , She, Wolf (fka Beauty in the Beast ), All of Us Are Dead Season 2 and Solo Leveling also appeared at the event, where Netflix outlined a series of stas to highlights its local impact.

Top non-English content

Netflix said Korean content was the most-watched non-English language content on the app and that over 80% of subscribers watch it. The streamer launched in the country on January 6, 2016.

The streamer noted flagged that more than 200 Korean titles had hit its Global Top 10 chart in the past five years, with Squid Game Season 1 unsurprisingly staying there the longest (32 consecutive weeks). Teach You a Lesson was noted as the tenth most-watched non-English title in the streamer’ history, with all three seasons of Squid Game in the top ten.

Other stats thrown out include working with more than 80 Korean production companies, filming taking place in more than 100 towns and cities, and a third of its originals being led by first-time writers and/or directors.

article_text:
Cine

JK Simmons ya habla de Justice League 2

Julio Vélez

Además de confirmar su presencia en The Batman como el comisionado Gordon, JK Simmons declaró que ya se está trabajando en Justice League 2.

Falta menos de un mes para que se estrene Justice League , pero el actor JK Simmons ya tiene algo que decir sobre el futuro del DCEU .

El intrérprete del actual comisionado Gordon charló para la revista Total Film de diciembre ( vía ) y dijo: “Pero esto es solo la primera película de Justice League –que esperamos sean unas cuantas más–. Ya están trabajando en los guiones para The Batman y la siguiente película de la Liga de la Justicia . Introducen mi encarnación como el comisionado Gordon. No tengo mucho qué hacer. Siento que ya me sumergí en quién es el comisionado Gordon”.

Esta sería la primera vez que alguien directamente relacionado con el DCEU habla de Justice League 2 . ¿Quién será el escritor encargado de la nueva historia? En este caso tendría que ser alguien diferente a Chris Terrio ( Argo, Justice League, Batman vs. Superman ), pues él ya está trabajando en Star Wars: Episode IX .

Por cierto, JK Simmons detalló que interpretar a Jim Gordon es tratar de llenar unos zapatos muy grandes, considerando a los grandes actores antes de él con el papel del directivo de policía de Ciudad Gótica. “Algunos actores realmente grandiosos han interpretado esa parte antes. Es como cuando todo mundo en Londres ha hecho a Hamlet. Ahora, es mi turno para ser Gordon”.

Justice League se estrenará el 17 de noviembre de 2017. ¿Será cierto el rumor de que Cinépolis no la tendrá en su cartelera (como sucedió con Suicide Squad y Cinemex hace meses)?

Julio Vélez Colaborador en web y revista Cine PREMIERE desde 2006. Me especializo en anime/manga, comics, doblaje, tecnología y videojuegos. Mis sagas favoritas: Doctor Who, Star Trek, Dragon Ball y Star Wars. Batimaníaco, geek ochentero y hardcore gamer.

article_text:
Bodies Of Light: Tori Amos

Bodies of Light is created from photographs I took of Tori Amos during the In Times Of Dragons tour. The series is made through an experimental process of light, movement, and long exposure.

These photographs are my attempt to give form to the mystery of artistic inspiration, the muses, and the unseen presences Tori Amos has long described as moving through her music and performances, and the ways those ideas take shape in my own mind’s eye through her work.

Her work has been a part of my creative life for more than thirty years. These photographs come not just from artistic inquiry, but from a deep affection for the artist and the work that has accompanied so much of my life. When I photographed her, my own artistic language unexpectedly collided with that history, and Bodies of Light came from the encounter. What began as an experiment with a single photograph unexpectedly developed into this large body of work.

These images also come from my lifelong intuitive way of perceiving. Since childhood, I have experienced what some call auras: color and energy that extends beyond the visible body. These photographs try to give visual form to the way that I perceive.

I approach each photograph without a predetermined outcome, working in-camera with light, movement, and duration. I remain open to whatever might emerge. The process becomes a form of photographic scrying: an intuitive search for what might reveal itself when likeness begins to loosen and the visible body becomes a threshold.

Through this process, the images move further from documentation and closer to the experience I am trying to hold: the feeling that, through her music and performances, she seems to give form to something larger than herself.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "S andra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. article_text:
S andra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)

And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says.

We are talking about Fatherland. Directed by acclaimed Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski, Hüller plays the German polymath Erika Mann, who in the film drives her novelist father Thomas Mann through newly divided postwar Germany. The Nazi past shadows everything – but the movie is also tied up with the birth of East Germany, where Hüller grew up. (She still lives in what was once the GDR.) I tell her I’ve never before seen a film that acknowledged the utopian dreams of that place and time, however damaged they became. Yes, she replies: German directors don’t know how to approach it.

“But Fatherland has a grief that you feel clearer coming from the East.”

And then her voice cracks, and she cries. We reflexively apologise to each other. “I’m just grateful Pawel gave space to this political idea that didn’t survive in Germany , but is one maybe people can still think about. The socialist idea.”

Hüller wipes her eyes. Finally, she laughs. “You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you? I can see the headline.”

And yet she has always been open about the nuance to the East Germany she remembers from childhood – a place defined by more than the Stasi men of cold war thrillers. “What fascinates me is that in East and West were two systems that for a certain time could have learned from each other.” She apologises again; I’m not sure why. “It is this situation we live in now. I feel like I’m on thin ice.”

Inevitably, we come to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The subject is doubly unavoidable in light of Fatherland. The Manns originally fled the country in 1933 and they would end up in the US. “It’s no secret there are similarities now,” Hüller says. “Fascism doesn’t arrive overnight. It gets here slowly, in little doses.” Her tone turns businesslike. “The question is what we do about it.”

We all contain multitudes, but Hüller more than most. At home in Leipzig, she is a co-founder of the experimental Farn Kollektiv theatre group; a politically engaged woman of 48, she is the single mother to a teenage daughter. She is also deadpan funny. An account of her excellent safety record as a driver is a comic treasure. “ That should be your headline. ‘Sandra Hüller – a clean licence.’”

She is also a movie actor with snowballing momentum. In 2024, she astonished twice over as the wife of the commandant of Auschwitz in The Zone of Interest and a woman suspected of murdering her husband in Anatomy of a Fall. The latter saw her Oscar-nominated. Now, after Project Hail Mary, Digger and Fatherland, there will also be Rose, a stark 17th century fable in which she plays a war veteran – who is, in fact, a woman passing as a man. Oscar talk is simmering once more. America is freshly excited.

“OK, so what is happening is that I made very different movies at different times, but they’re all coming out together. It’s nothing I control.” What is good, she says, is that, with her as the common thread, Hollywood marketing budgets end up spotlighting the likes of Fatherland too. “On the other hand, I struggle with seeing myself as someone special. I still consider myself part of a group. That is actually the highest praise I can give myself.”

Curiously, a collective spirit might also apply to the fifth film Hüller is strongly rumoured to be in this year: Marvel relaunch Avengers: Doomsday. Whatever else Marvel movies represent, they have a reputation for an oddly egalitarian vibe on set. I wonder aloud if that’s true. “Me too!” She gives an impish tilt of the head. Ah. For the record, then, Hüller still may or may not be part of the new Avengers.

But in theory, a Marvel film might feel unexpectedly non-hierarchical? “I heard that as well! Which would show having a lot of money available doesn’t have to mean abusing your power. And that would be a great thing. In theory.”

If the thought of Hüller doing Marvel takes getting used to, it makes more sense after Project Hail Mary. In a deft piece of Hollywood feelgood, she proved the perfect foil for Ryan Gosling’s reluctant spaceman as stone-faced mission controller Eva Stratt. The air of ultra-competence was very Sandra Hüller for Beginners. The film even harked back to her 2016 breakthrough in skewed German comedy Toni Erdmann. Hüller has a glorious singing voice. Then, she karaoked Whitney Houston’s Greatest Love of All. Now, it was Harry Styles’ Sign of the Times.

“But I think Eva Stratt made some people uncomfortable. It can feel unusual to be governed by a woman.”

Still, making Project Hail Mary was another pleasant surprise – her first Hollywood set where the directors – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller – actually lightened the mood. “They made sure we could actually play. Have fun.” She did, though, find it strange being wrangled by runners on the kind of blockbuster where producers want to know where a star is at all times. (Unlike almost every actor on her level, Hüller doesn’t even have an assistant.) “But you can always hide in the bathroom.”

Would she spend more time in the US than necessary? “Not right now. No. It’s a workplace.” Anyway, she says, she likes where she lives. “It’s simple. America is just very far away.” And she smiles.

She believes audiences embraced Project Hail Mary because the film-makers sought to unite them, inside a cinema at least. “And entertain them without the usual things – death and weapons. So you have a story about a human with a task that lets them be bigger than themselves. That inspired people.”

But what about their response to Digger? Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, with Tom Cruise as a cartoonish oil tycoon, the movie got poor reviews, then did cataclysmically at the box office. Can we talk about it? “Sure!” she says brightly. “I mean, we expected a strong reaction. It’s a polarising movie. And a political movie, which we weren’t able to say in interviews. For whatever reason.” A beat. “But personally – I was surprised by the harshness of the rejection. People really hated it!”

Hüller, though, says she loves it. “Years from now, it will be seen as a document of our times.” But time won’t be able to fix a problem like the thinness of her role as the sister of Cruise’s character. There should have been more of her, I say. “Well, there was.” Naturally, she smiles. Ah. (Again.) More rumours put forward that her role was heavily cut by Iñárritu. “You’d have to talk to Alejandro.” Are they still friendly? “Of course!”

At the movie’s royal gala premiere in London, the audience spent hours watching on screen the introductions of Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, to the cast and many others. I tell Hüller a cameraman briefly focused on her, waiting in a red carpet frock with a look that suggested a looming medical procedure. The memory clearly tickles her.

So what was she thinking? “Well, I thought of the people in the cinema, waiting for us to start the movie, and not being able to leave. Also, my feet really hurt.” But she has a surprise in store. “I mean, I’ve never met any royalty in my life, so I was also fangirling.” Really? Hüller seems an unlikely monarchist. “I don’t find the monarchy interesting. But they are fascinating, remarkable personalities.” So what did she finally talk about with the royal couple? “Oh, I can’t remember. I was in shock!” Would she like to meet them again? “Of course! I want to have tea with them! I want to talk about everything with them!”

Hüller is now hooting with laughter.

If we do include the Avengers, her fifth film of this most productive year is Rose. Like Fatherland, it is a story of the German past, in black and white. And yet, after fun with royals and Ryan Gosling, Rose now brings her back to modern Germany. It was filmed in Saxony-Anhalt, “where a certain party recently won power”. (This is the German state where the AfD claimed 43.8% of the vote in September.)

In preparation to play a character passing as male, Hüller says she watched men more closely than she ever had before. The result was a study of all that goes into being read as male. “Honestly, it left me astonished. I realised that as a woman, I rarely enter a room and think of it as a battleground. But male behaviour is so related to that. Where is the enemy and how can I defeat him?”

So do men make bad socialists? “No! Some of the most famous socialists have been men.” Could that be why we don’t have socialism, though? She grins and wags a finger. “You forgot Mamdani?” She also has a related point. “One advantage of being born in the GDR and seeing it fall apart, or reunified, however you want to call it, is you learn no system is for ever. And that is interesting in a time when the things we’ve done so long don’t work any more. So maybe it is good to think of different ways they could work in future.”

Hüller is having to rethink the present too. Despite still seeing herself as a theatre actor who sometimes makes films, her German stage career is now on hold – at least in front of the curtain. Fame complicates. “If you are part of an ensemble but people come to see you as if the others matter less, I don’t enjoy that.” But she has a workaround. Farn are now creating two new plays she will instead direct. (“One is about revenge. The other goodbyes.”) So far, she says, the new role has been a pleasure. “I love the discussions. I love watching people invent. And we will see how long this wave continues.”

She tells me she is also curious how my piece will turn out. In Germany, she says, interview subjects give notes on a draft before anything goes to print. We don’t do that in the UK, I say. “I know. But as the interviewed person, it gives you a feeling of being respected. Not that I don’t feel respected here. Anyway, I never change much.” She smiles. “Sometimes just a comma.” So will she read this? “No, because I have no say.”

And yes, she agrees, laughing, that means I can write whatever I want.

translated_excerpt_zh: 新电影《祖国》带了桑德拉·海勒回一个分裂的德国,她谈论破坏的梦想,好莱坞感觉好,而在新电影《玛威尔》中出现的桑德拉·海勒哭泣,感觉很奇怪。

editorial_excerpt_zh: 世上有各种“圣杯”，然后还有《恶魔》。尽管肯·罗素这部拍摄于1971年的电影几十年来一直以某种形式存在，但许多人（比如我）总是避开它——不是因为它的丑闻内容，而是因为缺少了这些内容。作为极少数在导演剪辑版DVD时代未能得到妥善修复的制片厂电影之一，它长久以来似乎注定要在电影炼狱中徘徊。

And we had sort of done a partial fix by getting the footage and showing that the film could be assembled in a version. So on the one hand: I’m immensely proud and I’m immensely happy that it’s happened; and on the other hand, there’s just a part of me that thinks, “Okay, how did we get…?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The honest truth of it is: we got here because Spencer [Collantes] and Christian [Parkes] arrived at Warner Bros. and said, “We really want to do The Devils .” And because of the work that they had done at NEON… look, I am a 63-year-old man, right? Me obsessing about The Devils it’s like, “Yeah, well, I knew Ken. I promised Ken that we’d do this.” You know, “Okay, that’s fine, that’s just Mark being Mark, you know.” When Spencer and Christian—off the work thing, the success that they had at Neon—came to us and said, “We really want to do The Devils ,” I think that they went, “Oh, okay.” They’re smart. They’ve got their ear to the ground. They’ve got their finger on the pulse of what is happening now, which I don’t have; I’m an old man. And I think that that’s what changed, was that the kind of lack of enthusiasm for The Devils , which had really kind of dogged it throughout its history, was turned around by Spencer and Christian saying, “You know…” That’s a terrible phrase, but they’re young gunslingers and they come into town and go, “We think The Devils is really important.” And I think that they went, “Okay.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "From what I understand, and correct me if I’m wrong, but [WB] were nothing but supportive. And what it took was for them just to hear the right people say, “We think this is a really good idea.” And then, suddenly, it was a really good idea. Then there’s part of me that goes, “Oh, it was that simple.” It reminds me of the bit at the end of The Wizard of Oz when she says, “Yeah, you always had the ability to go home.” “The whole time?” Yeah. That’s what it took."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NYFF64-2026-The_Devils-Sean_DiSerio-009-1-1200x800.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mark Kermode and Lisi Tribble at the 64th New York Film Festival. Photo by Sean DiSerio."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bit of a deus ex machina. Me being as a cinephile, you have your white whales, the movies that you never get to see or you never get to see in their purest form. Like, a lot of people are haunted by the thought of the longer Magnificent Ambersons , for instance, or like, last year I got to see one of my white whales, which is Patrick Tims’ Love Massacre , when it premiered at the Tokyo International Film Festival. And sometimes there’s that feeling where you finally see it and it’s not disappointing per se, but it is also a movie and a fixed runtime, and then it’s over, right? Which I think is maybe what partly what you’re getting at a little bit, that feeling of you can’t believe it and then suddenly it’s just happening."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, but I don’t feel like it’s just a movie and a runtime and then it’s over. I kind of feel like it’s out in the world finally. I mean, you’ve got to remember: I have thought about this for a really long time. I mean, not as long as Ken did, obviously"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For about a really, really long time. And every time, I mean… when I saw it in the Cannes premiere and it just looked astonishing. I mean, it just looked amazing. I hadn’t seen the restored version until it was in Cannes. And I was sitting there with Lisi [Tribble, Ken Russell’s widow] and we were both looking at each other going, “Did you know?” And I am really looking forward to tomorrow night. And somebody said to me, “You’re going to watch it again?” “Yes. Yes.” I’ve only seen it this good once. I now need to sit. I’d seen it 25, 30 times in the late-night circuit when I was watching the film and some old 35mm print in some butchered version. So, there’s no sense to me of, you know, “That’s it. It’s done now. It’s finished.” What I feel like is “That’s it. It’s done now. It’s beginning.” And what I really am excited to know is what happens now."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What will happen is that I will keep going back and seeing it every time. There’ll now be the release thing that would be great, and I will keep going back to see it because there is something about it as a complete film now that is the beginning of a story rather than the end of a story. And part of me thinks, what would it have been like if the film had been released like this in 1971?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Right."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Would people have understood it better? Would it have made more sense? I don’t, I don’t know. It was in one of the interviews I did earlier today, somebody said, “It’s like the film was waiting for the world to catch up with it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Definitely."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And I think the world hasn’t quite caught up with it yet. I think it’s closer than it was before. It was funny because of when Billy Friedkin did the re-cut of The Exorcist for “the version you’d never seen,” that I had written about the missing scenes, and the last sentence of the book that I wrote for the BFI about The Exorcist was —paraphrasing—we can only be tantalized by Bill Blatty’s suggestion that there was a better version of the film. And I took the line from—me being a hack—but I took the line from the publicity of the film: I said, “That thought is almost beyond comprehension” because the tagline for the film was, “Something almost beyond comprehension is happening to a girl in this house.” Dot, dot, dot—you know, dramatic flourish."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And then the stuff got put back in again. And that’s what I know about the closure thing: you go, “Oh, there we are.” There we are. And then people now said to me, “Well, is it better?” And the answer is, “No, it’s different.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Okay."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Okay, it’s different. It’s not better, it’s different.” In the case of The Devils , is it better? Yes. It is. It was damaged goods before. It had a big problem before because it was damaged. And now it isn’t damaged anymore. So, it’s not like in the case of The Exorcist —there wasn’t that sense of closure that you’re talking about. “Oh, okay, that’s it. That’s the thing that I was dreaming about.” In the case of this, I always knew that there was something wrong with it because the first time I ever spoke to Ken about it, he said to me, “It’s damaged goods.” That was the phrase that he used. He said, because they just took this stuff out of it, that left it with a hole. Something is damaged about it, and then you put it back in and go, “No, that is better. That is what it always should have looked like.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Right."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And John Phillips—the theologian—said, fascinatingly, when he first saw the film, it was in Ken’s cut with the Rape of Christ sequence in it. And he said, “Despite the fact that that sequence was cut out, and it was never in the film from the release until now,” he said, in his mind, it was always there, because in his mind, it was part of the film. It was like, you know, it was."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I get it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“But the rest of us had to wait to see what it was meant to look like.” So I kind of feel like now, after all this time, it’s finally being released for the first time. It’s like the things that people have seen of it up until now are sort of a trailer, but this is actually the film."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, that’s so pretentious. I’m so sorry."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "No, no, no, I think that’s great. I mean, because I think you’re speaking with enthusiasm. And I think sometimes enthusiasm and pretension get confused for each other. I want to circle back, because this is all on my mind, as you’re saying, “This is what the film should have looked like.” What was the DigiBeta of it?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So the DigiBeta that we had in 2000—in, whatever it was, 2000—when we were making Hell on Earth , we had found the missing scenes. We had found the reel of film that had the missing scenes on it, and we had digitized that. And we had put those scenes in Hell on Earth . So the first time the missing scenes were ever shown was on the Channel 4 documentary Hell on Earth , in which we had all those scenes in. The DigiBeta was a digital version of the British X-rated version, which had sort of disappeared from view, because the film opened in the UK with the British X rating. It was then further cut for the American version. So the American version was always shorter than the British version."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Okay, I see."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After the film had done its first run in cinemas, the British X-rated prints seemed to disappear and be superseded by the American R-rated prints. So for example: when I first saw the film, which was in either ’79 or ’80, either the winter of ’79 or… oh, the spring of ’80, the version that I saw, the version that was on the late-night circuit, was the American R-rated version. It had a British exit certificate at the beginning of it, but it wasn’t the British version; it was the American R-rated version. In fact, the British X-rated version was pretty much out of circulation until the late 1990s."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So we had the DigiBeta of the film in its most complete version, which was the British X-rated version. It was that version into which Mike Bradwell, who was the editor of both The Devils and of our documentary, re-inserted the two key sequences, which is the Rape of Christ sequence and the sequence with Sister Jeanne and the bone. But it was a digital video. So when we projected it onto screen one of the National Film Theater, it looked like a video projection. I mean, it was good, but it was a video."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And the time that you noticed it the most was in those scenes when Grandier is addressing the crowd and the walls of Loudun, the white walls and the tiling inside. You know what Digi looks like?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I do. Terrible."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It goes a bit squiggly. And you were looking at it thinking, “It’s like watching it through a glass darkly. I can see that there… I can see that there is a brilliant thing there, but it’s.. it’s slightly obscured.” But what was fascinating was: at least you could see that that was what the film was meant to look like, but you had to kind of make the sort of leap of imagination as to what it would look like."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When we finally saw the restoration, it was… I mean, Guillermo Del Toro has said this. It’s like, what was the comparison that he used? He said it was like cleaning the Sistine Chapel with saliva. And it was like, it was literally like, “Oh,” because: right. I quote this all the time, my friend Nigel Floyd, the film critic, says this thing the documentary Hell on Earth , and it’s my favorite comment about The Devils , and I repeat it all the time and people look at me like I’m being foolish. He said the thing about it is: it is a film which is a film. And what he meant by that is: it’s a film that is not a script. It is a film that is a film. It being a film quality was what it looked like."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Right."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And so up until the point of the restoration, it hadn’t actually looked like… so when it was first out in pristine print, fine, but the pristine prints were cut. And so therefore, there was something missing. Then when we finally restored it, fine, it had the rhythm, but it was from a DigiBeta. So finally, after all this time of imagining it, “Oh, that’s what it looks like.” And the Cannes thing was literally like we were just all sitting there going… I’ve imagined it, but it’s there. It’s better, or even better because you can’t quite describe—I can’t, because I’m not very good with words—you can’t quite describe in words what it does, because it is a film which is a film. Does that make any sense at all?"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/5-Ken-Russells-The-Devils-Key-Set-1200x817.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Behind the scenes of The Devils"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, it’s funny. This resonates exactly with two things I was thinking while I was seeing the film. One is, like I said, sometimes when you encounter the white whale, it’s because it’s finally been restored. Other times, it’s a movie that you do know well, but you’ve only seen it on DVD or VHS, and when you see the restoration—I’ve had this thought multiple times—you literally didn’t know it could look like that."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, fine. You said it better."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Like, I thought it was embossed in amber as what the film looks like, and then… that’s insanely gratifying. But also the thing you say about “a film that looks like a film,” which is that I love all kinds of cinema, and I know that sometimes there’s a place for grandiosity, sometimes there’s a place for the homemade. But it kind of brought me back to this experience, with all that being said, of when I saw the final cut of Apocalypse Now at the Beacon Theater here in New York, which is a… I mean, it’s not even really a movie theater, that’s how big the screen is."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Okay."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And you’re sitting there and you’re watching it, and there’s something about a solidity of the image, on an image-by-image basis, of a certain force of detail, which, now I’m sounding pretentious. But there is something about that experience of: this is made in such a way, with such a density of image that goes beyond what we usually think of in film. I think especially as cinephiles, there’s this idea of sometimes you fetishize the thing that looks ugly or small, because that’s more dignified than something that’s big and grand."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, yeah, yeah."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But a movie like The Devils for me, those two streams cross."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yes, I think that’s right. So the final cut of Apocalypse Now , does it have the plantation stuff in it? Does it have—"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It does."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fine. Okay."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And it was a great experience seeing it, because it was at the premiere, so nobody had seen it, and you could feel the air kind of suck out of the room when people realized it was going to stay in."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That’s interesting."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I kind of like that scene, and he also did a good job saying, like, “I like it too,” because he did a Q&A after. He was like, “I like it too, I want to keep it in.” But it was a funny experience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, yeah, yeah. The interpolation thing is… I mean, the point you’re making about the sort of the deeper thing about looking at the image—you said it better than I did—the solidity of it, there’s something about Ken’s filmmaking when he is, and actually this kind of relates slightly to Apocalypse Now , it is very hard now to imagine a filmmaker being funded to make a film as out-there as The Devils was, because The Devils does not look like a film that anyone sat around and workshopped. Ken wrote the script for The Devils in a matter of weeks. He literally sat down and it came out of him, like he had the two books, he had the Whiting and he had the Huxley, and he just wrote. And then he had access to these sets and the sets were big, and it was a very, very big kind of ballroom set. And then he has access to the very finest acting talent—Oliver Reed, Vanessa Redgrave, Dudley Sutton, Michael Rainsford, and Georgina Hale. It’s extraordinary."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And then he has Peter Maxwell Davies doing the score, like literally the cutting-edge avant-garde composer of his stuff. All these things and then the costume by Shirley Russell, all these things together, it is hard to imagine a studio doing that again now. The only comparison I can think of is—recently, for example—Paul Thomas Anderson made One Battle After Another , and everyone was going, “It is astonishing that they allowed that amount of money to be spent on a movie that’s that adventurous.” And, okay, did well, but it’s a risk."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the case of The Devils , it’s like: the thing that is really remarkable about it is, it is a film that looked like, when he made it, was untrammeled. And then once he’d done it, they went, “No, no, no, sorry. No, no, no.” And then they had to start taking bits out of it, whereas now you’d think what would happen in advance is: you wouldn’t be able to make it in the first place. I don’t know. Maybe things are changing, because you hear people talking now about studios actually returning to a kind of auteur-driven thing, but it was a singular vision of a singular filmmaker who made films that were in a style that was very much his own, and he was allowed to do it, and then it was messed up after the fact."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/The-Devils-Continuity-Photo-1-1200x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/The-Devils-Continuity-Photo-3-1200x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/The-Devils-Continuity-Photo-6-1200x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/The-Devils-Continuity-Photo-4-1200x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/The-Devils-Continuity-Photo-2-1200x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/The-Devils-Continuity-Photo-5-1200x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Behind-the-scenes contiunity photos from The Devils."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I mean, there was applause in the end credits for Derek Jarman, too, from the audience, and it sort of begets the question: why isn’t every film set designed by someone of Jarman’s caliber?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, partly because not every filmmaker who’s making a a fairly decently budgeted studio movie would have the guts that Ken had, because the way that Ken got Derek Jarman—Ken told me this story—was he said that a friend of his had said, “I was on a train, I met this guy called Derek Jarman, he’s really interesting, I know you’re looking for a new look on The Devils , you should go see him.” So Ken goes, “Okay.” So Ken goes to Derek Jarman’s studio, which is on the banks of the Thames, and it’s this great big warehouse, and he walks in and it’s freezing cold, and in the middle of it, there is a greenhouse with Derek Jarman sitting in it with a two-bar electric fire, and all the way around the walls are this exhibition of his see-through Cardinal’s coats, and one of them’s filled with dollars, and one of them’s filled with stuff that he found washed up in the Thames, and one of them’s, you know…"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And Ken looks at these things, and he goes, “This guy’s got ideas,” and he sits, and he talks to Derek Jarman for hours, and he just goes, “Yep, him. Him. Come and design this massive studio production that we’re making at Pinewood Studios, in which we’re literally going to build Loudun. Do that.” That is the risk. It’s like, not only did Ken take the risk—he was able to take the risk. He was able to go, “Yeah, I’m going to make this movie with this guy. You haven’t heard of him, but I think he’s a genius.” I was talking to somebody earlier on, saying there is an argument for saying that The Devils is Derek Jarman’s first feature, right? Because it is a Derek Jarman movie in the same way that it’s a Ken Russell movie. And it’s funny now that everybody celebrates the thing about, “You know, it’s Derek Jarman,” and his name comes across the screen every because, of course, it’s Derek Jarman, but at the time, nobody knew who Derek Jarman was—he was just Ken thought, “No, he’s brilliant, he’ll do it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, if it was very similar to it in minimalist, people would see Derek Jarman at the end and go, “Oh. Oh, strange, okay.” A few things to branch off from there, but I watched this video of you and Russell doing a Q&A about the film probably 20 or so years ago, and towards the end there’s an interesting conversation you guys had about the concept of kitsch."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And he said, which I think is a good quote, “Kitsch is fine.” And you’re also talking about the film coming out now and you’re wondering how the response is going to be. This not just advocate, but this kind of shepherd for the film, do you feel confident about how a fresh audience is going to respond to it? Or is confidence not even part of it? Is concern not part of it? It goes into the world and people respond how they do?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, I’ll be honest with you: I am incredibly bullheaded. Right? I have always thought it was a masterpiece, sure. And I have never understood anyone not thinking that. Ken and I bonded when I first met him because it’s quite easy to bond with somebody who tells you that the film that you’ve made that caused you no manner of trouble, just goes, “No, I think it’s a work of genius and I think you’re a genius and I think it’s a masterpiece and I think we have to put it back together again and fix it.” There is no part of me that doubts for one minute that the film is a masterpiece. I have been very aware of the fact that it was a wrongly maligned masterpiece, of which there have been many over the history of cinema. I’ve never, ever doubted that it was anything other than a masterpiece. The real delight has been this sort of growing groundswell of other voices saying the same thing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So some time ago, Sight and Sound did one of those polls of everyone’s favorite movies. There were only two people then who put The Devils in their top 10. It was me, and the other one was Alex Cox. And that was 20, however many years ago it was. And then over the years, other voices start to join in, and then when we did the restoration, at the end people were very interested and then Guillermo [Del Toro] is talking about his love for Ken Russell—as a longstanding love for Ken Russell. So okay, there’s a rising tide of voices that the film is much better than perhaps its initial review. So by the time we get to this point, it’s like I’m thinking, “Everyone who knows anything knows that the film is a masterpiece. And if you don’t think it’s a masterpiece, you’re wrong.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But when we got to Cannes, there is the moment just before the film starts, and then it comes on the screen, and literally it comes on the screen with the theatrical production of the Venus thing, and you can hear people going, “Sorry, which film is this? The opening… is this how The Devils opens?” Because people think of the play; they don’t think of that. And so after that Cannes screening, the response was so rapturous, it was just like, “Oh, well, there we go. Of course. There we are. That’s it.” But there’s no part of me that feels any nervousness about how it will… I’m sure that there will be some people who will react negatively to it, some people will react positively to it, as is always the case with any movie at all. But I have no doubt that it is a film that will command serious attention and will be taken seriously, as it always should have been."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But that’s partly because I am very pigheaded, and I have believed that since I first saw it. I mean, there was a lot of bad stuff written about The Devils . Reviews when it first came out accused it of all manner of terrible things. And you read the BBFC reports, they thought it was disgraceful and disgusting, and you go, “No, it isn’t. It is a work of art.” And so yeah, no: I don’t feel any anxiety or worry about it at all. I was delighted by how it played in Cannes, but I kind of think like the world has caught up with it and that, if I’m really honest with you, the way that I feel right now is smug. “See? They flew you across the ocean to be here.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You should be. You know, anytime I get put on a paid flight, I’m feeling so smug. And I’m not getting the honors."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But it is just that kind of thing. It’s just like, “See? There’s the evidence, right?” Because there were times when I was at Time Out in the 1980s, one of my editors said to me once, “Your problem is that you don’t believe that there is such a… you think…” No, the exact phrase was, said, “Your problem is that you believe that all art is redeemable.” And I said, “What do you—what do you even mean by that?” And they said, “Well, you just, you believe things.” And they were speaking, as it happened, about a conversation we had about Caligula , right? Because I had said somewhere in the middle of the car crash of a movie that is Caligula , there is a half-decent film struggling to get out. Well, I don’t know whether you saw the Caligula recut from a couple of years ago."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I did not."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s really good. And I did an interview with Malcolm McDowell, because over the years I had been involved in sort of various [ways]. Now, Caligula is never going to be a masterpiece. I’m not comparing The Devils to Caligula , but there was something in there, which was really Malcolm McDowell’s performance. And I had interviewed Malcolm McDowell, and he had talked about the heartbreak of it, that he had given this performance, and then it had turned into Caligula —this spectacular car crash of a film. And then when this new recut finally got done—it was a couple of years ago; two, three years ago—he said for the first time ever, he was able to go, “ See ? That’s what I thought we were doing.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And so there’s part of me that just thinks when you—having said for such a long time that The Devils is a masterpiece—I never said Caligula was a masterpiece. Having said for a long time that The Devils is a masterpiece—it is Ken Russell’s best film, it is Ken Russell’s most underrated and misunderstood film—and now I literally feel like going, “ See ?” Sorry. When you transcribe this, it will just be Mark saying “ See ” over and over again."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I think the emphasis on it will be good. I mean, it’s funny because you met Russell in the mid-90s, which means you probably knew him for the last 15 or so years of his life. There’s an interesting question about the filmmaker-critic relationship. I think it’s interesting because you are very renowned as a critic, but you also have historian, advocate—there are a few hats that I think you wear. And how does your relationship with a director’s filmography change when you form your relationship with the director? It’s not like you necessarily love or even like every film that they’ve made, but are you looking at their films through a particular, different lens once you know them as a person?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So when I met Ken in 1995, his feature-film career had pretty much finished. At that point, he was what he referred to as a “garagist” because he made films in his garage. And he made independent films that were, like, absolutely independently funded because he couldn’t get money to make features. He didn’t have ideas—he did, but the British film industry was not very kind to Ken in his later years. So by the time I met him, the body of work existed substantially in terms of his feature films. And I knew what I thought about those films, because I had seen The Devils and Tommy and Women in Love and Music Lovers and Marlor and The Devils and Crimes of Passion and I had seen all the films, and I knew what I thought about them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So it wasn’t like I was going to meet Ken and it was going to radically change the way I thought about the films, because I already kind of knew how I did think about them. The other thing was that, despite the fact that I knew Ken pretty well over the 15 years, I never stopped being a fan. I couldn’t quite believe that we were going round to Ken’s house. I couldn’t quite believe that I was on first-name terms with Ken. I mean, it was like literally for 15, 16 years, I had to keep pinching myself and going, “It’s Ken Russell in my kitchen.” You know, “We’re going to the pub with Ken Russell. I’m doing an onstage with Ken Russell.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Absolutely."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And although people find it quite hard to believe, the same was true of Billy Friedkin. I never, ever got over the fact that Billy, he gave me a copy of, I think, the Cruising soundtrack, and he wrote a thing in it, which said, you know, “Thanks for all your support over the years, and your friendship.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And I was like, “Are we friends?” You know, but because the imbalance was never going away. It was never going because he was—he was Billy Friedkin. He made The Exorcist and Sorcerer and films that were really, really good. Now, that didn’t mean that I loved everything he did. I didn’t. There were plenty of films that he made that weren’t to my liking. I didn’t like The Guardian one bit. I didn’t like Deal of the Century , an absolute mess of a film. Total mess of a film. I mean, it’s a weird thing, because Billy always said, “Yeah, it was a great script,” but it… and you think, “Really?” But so he made plenty of films that I didn’t like. It didn’t matter. It didn’t in any way affect what I thought about him as a filmmaker, and it didn’t affect what he thought about me, because it wasn’t like he didn’t know, because the stuff was all published. So there were some films of his that I really liked that he couldn’t quite understand why I really liked them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Right."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So in the case of Ken, there are things that Ken did that, I think that we know, are more important than some other things that he did. But when you look at some of the later work, like Lair of the White Worm is now a film that people really love as a cult movie."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/4-Ken-Russells-The-Devils-Key-Set-1192x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Devils"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It shows up on streaming every October for horror programming."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And I bet people watch it and go, “Wow, you ever seen Lair of the White Worm ?” And that was a film which, when it first came out, people didn’t think, “Oh, that’s a film that’s going to last, however many years it’s been.” But now it is an absolute die-hard cult classic. And I think that probably when I first met Ken and we talked about his movies, that wasn’t one of the movies that I talked to him about, because I was talking to him about Women in Love and The Devils and all the rest of it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I see."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But even when, after all those years we had known each other, I was still a Ken Russell fanboy. So I don’t think it fundamentally changed anything because if somebody is a great filmmaker and they make a bad film, it doesn’t make them a bad filmmaker."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And one of the things that people say is like, “Well, if you like a filmmaker, then you are much more inclined to be kind to their work.” To which the answer is: “Yeah. That’s how it works.” If you think that somebody is an admirable filmmaker and they make a bad film, it’s more interesting than if somebody who isn’t an admirable filmmaker makes a bad film because people’s failures are kind of interesting. If you believe that the intent, the intention, the artistic ambition is worthy, that does affect how you think about films. So yes: when people say, “Well, you tend to be kinder to the films of directors that you like,” yeah, but it’s not I like them personally. I got to know them because I like their work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And that’s the case with both Billy Friedkin and with Ken Russell: I got to know them because I was obsessed with their work, and I wrote about their work, and then I was privileged to meet them and make documentaries about them. As a result of that, we had a relationship that, on one level, you could define as a friendship, but on another level—and Ken, God bless him, was really good about this. He knew that if he was going to spend an evening with Mark, half of that evening was going to be taken up with Mark going, “Now, Ken, tell me: when you did Women in Love , what lenses were you using with that?” That requires a certain amount of patience, because as anybody who is a great artist knows, you don’t necessarily want to be surrounded by your greatest fan. It must get quite annoying."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chris Farley and Paul McCartney."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, I’ve caught myself doing it too."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, and it’s really hard not to. Because it’s Ken Russell and you’re just having a nice time, and then you go, “Okay, you know that scene in Altered States …”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What you’re saying about the “fundamentally more interesting”—I mean, that’s point origin for a concept of auteurism, as Truffaut wrote about it before he ever shot a frame of film. He said, a bad film by a great filmmaker is more interesting than any… and I think you still see people blanch at that a little bit, and I think it’s interesting because it gets into this level of… it’s not about biases necessarily, or lowering your critical faculties, but I think it’s this strange median point between critical faculties and a sort of unbridled enthusiasm. It’s this weird place where they meet."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah. But I honestly think that one of the things I find very hard is the idea of objective criticism. Criticism is not objective, right? It is personal. Now, there are things about it that are objective: being factually correct about a movie. Like, one of the things that Ken was so incensed about Alex Walker’s review of The Devils in the Evening Standard —and you know the famous story that Alex Walker really didn’t like the film—Ken was incensed because there were two things that Alex Walker said in the review that did not happen in the film. One of them was that we see Grandier’s penis being crushed. We don’t. It doesn’t happen; it doesn’t happen. So they were on a late-night BBC talk show and Ken said to Alex Walker, “You’ve said these things in this review and they’re not true.” Alex wasn’t having any of it. So Ken lost his temper and he got up and he smacked Alex Walker over the head with his own review of the film and walked off. This was then a kind of a subject of great, great scandal—of course it was. But the thing that outraged him wasn’t that Alex Walker didn’t like the film; it’s that he said things about it that weren’t true."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure. Of course."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And so there are things that are objectively true, right? Who directed the film? Who wrote the film? How did the film get made? Then there are things which are objectively true about placing it within the context and the industry of other versions—is it a remake? Is it a novel adaptation? Where does it sit? There are other things which are objectively true about it, which is: it is this long, or it is this long, it was cut, or it wasn’t. These are objective, actual truths. Beyond that, how you respond to it is nothing but personal. And I find it very… the older I get—and I am very old—the more I think that the only way of being honest about it is to be honest about how personal it is."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I agree ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There was always something that was very difficult about writing for the Monthly Film Bulletin —that they said, “You need to write objectively.” And I tried really hard, but it was like: it was a lie. Me writing objectively was me trying to pretend that something that I thought was objectively true—it’s not objectively true, it’s subjectively true. This is how I respond to the film. And that is what all film criticism is. That’s why opinions differ about things, because everything is subjective. There are things that are objectively, factually correct, true, and then there are things which are your opinions.
