And the only way you can do that honestly is to be honest about how personal they are, because films are a very personal thing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the reasons that film censorship is quite complicated is because it works on a principle that you can predict how people react to material, broadly speaking, and you can’t. People react strangely to different things, particularly to a sin, to a medium as kind of as vibrant as cinema. This is a very long way of saying that in the end, for me, it’s all personal. It’s all to do with: I attach my affections to films that touch me in a certain way, and I hope that I describe them in a way that makes that make sense, even if you don’t agree with a single word of it. So you can go, “Okay, well, Kermode likes it. But then, of course Kermode likes it.” And even when that comes down to “Kermode,” I said, “Well, of course he likes it, because he likes Ken Russell.” That in itself is a valid criticism, because yes: I do like Ken Russell, and if you understand that I like Ken Russell, that is partly an explanation of why it is that I like the film, because I like the artistic swing, I like the… I like the intent."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And some films are made with more of what I would consider to be valid intent, and some films, there’s no part of me that thinks that when Michael Bay was making the Transformers movies, that he was inspired by a desire to tell those stories in the best possible, life-changing way. I don’t know, because I never met the guy."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But when I look at them, they just look like bank balances. They just look like a bunch of numbers."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NYFF64-2026-The_Devils-Sean_DiSerio-006-1-1200x800.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mark Kermode and Lisi Tribble at the 64th New York Film Festival. Photo by Sean DiSerio."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah. I mean, I think that’s a perfectly valid way of summarizing what’s a very difficult concept that seems like it’s always swimming around. As a way of closing the circle on this—this dream has been fulfilled, and it’s been fulfilled in a way that I think is beyond anybody’s, like I said, six months ago I wouldn’t have thought I’d be sitting there watching a 35mm print to this in its version. With that in mind, what, if anything, is second on the list of “White Whale, I want to see it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, I don’t know."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I also understand if there’s a hundred things tied for second place."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There almost isn’t. It’s partly an age thing. It’s partly what you refer to as my “white whales” have sailed. I saw The Exorcist and The Devils together on a late-night double bill in 1979. I saw them both on the same evening, right? That is probably the formative experience of my cinema-going life: those two films, one after the other. And then I have obsessed about those two films henceforth. Those two films now exist in the versions—as you said, The Exorcist exists in two versions. One of them is different to the other one. The Devils now exists in the version that it should have existed in. There isn’t anything else that’s burning up, and also because there isn’t anything else that has obsessed me that much over the years. [Note: after our interview, Mark would note that his white whale would be a remastered director’s cut of William Peter Blatty’s The Exorcist III .]"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So I’m kind of probably done. I mean, I’m 63. I’m not going to discover another thing now that I’ve got to, that I’m going to be obsessed about for 30 years. So no: I’m probably, in terms of those things, I’m done, and that’s fine. I’m just very, very pleased that this came about and we got to see it. My only regret is I wish Ken had been here to see it, and I do, but I do think that when the film is projected in an auditorium with an audience, he sort of is, sure. And I do believe that. I do think that there is something transcendent about that experience. But I wish he’d been there; I wish he’d been able to be there so that we could all go, “ See ?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I do. I’ve seen this film, I want to spend more time with the films of Ken Russell, which I haven’t spent as much time with as, admittedly, I should. And so it’s like that saying: You die twice—the first time is your body, the second time is the last time somebody says your name."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oh, I didn’t know that. Wow."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, that’s an old saying. And how many times is Ken Russell’s name being said today and tomorrow night?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, I do think it’s the start of something. I do genuinely think it’s the start of something. I think it’s like this is the birth of The Devils , and if it leads people back to the back catalog—I mean, there’s so much to discover. There is so many great films in there. And there are films that you’ll love, and films that you’ll hate, and films that you’ll be baffled by, and films that you’ll be dazzled by, and films that you will come out afterwards and go to the pub and have really heated discussions about what was going on."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I mean, I love Altered States . I absolutely love Altered States . The first time I saw Altered States was in the Empire Leicester Square in the West End of London, and I absolutely love every minute of it. And then I read some reviews of it, like, “Did we see the same film?” No. It was just, like, I couldn’t—I couldn’t quite understand, and then as I said, everything is personal, everything is. You like Altered States ? It’s a great film. The human spirit, the whole thing about the tangible encounter and “I’m going to find the fucker.” Ken and Lisi once did this thing which—they had lines from Ken’s film on ticker tape, and they would give them to people as a gift, and they gave me “And I’m going to find the fucker.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And in a way, you have found the fucker."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And, well, I have found the fucker—yeah."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Uncut and restored, The Devils opens in theaters on Friday, October 16."}]
article_text:
There are holy grails, and then there’s The Devils . While Ken Russell’s 1971 film has been available in some form or another for decades, many (like me) always avoided it—not for its scandalous content, but for the lack of such. In a rare class of studio films that passed through the era of director’s cut DVDs without proper restoration, it’s long seemed destined for cinematic purgatory.

That has changed in a manner so drastic it’s like everybody’s making up for lost time. With the creation of their new label, Clockwork, Warner Bros. announced a restoration of the full, uncut iteration for widespread release on 35mm that was preceded by a splashy Cannes world premiere that sold out in seconds. It happened in no small part because of The Devils ’ biggest champion, Mark Kermode, who has spent decades on the front line for Russell’s vision. With Kermode in town for a U.S. premiere at the New York Film Festival, I had the pleasure of partaking in a long, impassioned conversation with (literally) one of the most famous voices in film.

Two notes: 1) Kermode told me after our conversation that his white whale is a complete restoration of the director’s cut of William Peter Blatty’s The Exorcist III ; 2) at some point I misuse the term “begs the question.” I could feel myself making the mistake in real time, yet it slipped out. We regret the error.

Listen to or read our conversation below and subscribe here .

Music courtesy of Lex Walton : “Love Theme from an Unreleased Film” from the album Giving It Up .

The Film Stage: After years and years and hours and hours of hearing your voice, it’s nice to meet you.

Mark Kermode: I can only apologize.

It’s a good voice. I think if you had a bad voice, you wouldn’t have the career you’ve had.

Well, thank you. Well, when I was a kid, my father only ever gave me two pieces of advice, which was: “Learn to speak properly and stop watching all those films.” So I think that I ended up making a living speaking improperly about all those films was a bit of a crushing disappointment to him.

I was going to say 50% and that’s better than a lot of parent-child expectations.

Yeah.

The publicist asked me what I think is probably like a big question today, which is: have you seen The Devils before?

Have I seen it before?

No, have I seen…

Oh, yeah, sorry, yes. [Laughs] I thought you…

It’s crazy if you’ve…

Yeah, that would be wild, wouldn’t it? I’ve been bluffing all day. I’ve been doing really well.

And the answer that I had for her was: before the press screening on Tuesday, I hadn’t. And I hadn’t exactly because I was waiting for the occasion of Tuesday, which is the full version, uncut, in a theater; it being on a 35mm print was actually more than I would have reasonably hoped for even six months ago. Right? And it was a very special experience. I mean, you know as well as anybody how important where you sit in the theater can be. I sat in the front row of the Walter Reade, which is a good front row because it gives you enough space. But I sat in the front row to the side.

Is that where it is tomorrow night? Is that the Walter? Because I haven’t been in there yet. But I hear it’s a very good auditorium.

Yeah. It’s my favorite theater in New York.

Okay, great. And they say that there’s not a bad seat in the house.

I don’t think there is.

Great.

Front row to the side, it’s like this. And, probably from the first shot, I was just aware this was worth the wait, essentially. So this is an amazing occasion. Just doing the early research, I Googled “Mark Kermode The Devils.”

Okay.

And there comes up this YouTube video, “What To Do About The Devils “ from 2014.

Right.

Where you’re talking about the problem that exists at hand. Now that it’s here, what are some of the feelings that you have outside of the obvious “I’m happy it’s here,” the sense of the history that has been resolved, the sense of it’s going to be seen by people, now that you’ve had the experience of actually premiering it, like where’s your head at with it?

Well, partly, I still keep pinching myself because I can’t quite believe it’s happening. When the premiere happened at Cannes, which was in May, I was there with and I introduced the film with Lisi, Ken’s wife. And both Lisi and I had a moment before the film started, which was: we looked at each other and went, “Is this actually happening?” Because we had become so convinced that it would not happen. And so part of me is still kind of like, I’m still delighted, but also kind of slightly disbelieving that it’s happening because it has been such a long time. I first met Ken in ’95. I said to him, “Oh, we’ll find the missing scenes,” and he said, “No, you won’t. They’re gone, you know, they’re gone. They’re lost.” We found the missing scenes, in the beginning of the 21st century. We had them in a documentary in 2002. We had them in the DigiBeta, director’s cut in 2004. That was 22 years ago. So 22 years passed, that 2014 was like midway between them, and I think that we had all just resigned ourselves to the fact that it wasn’t going to happen, that what was going to happen was what had happened—that we had done the DigiBeta restoration, but that was that was the end of it. And honestly, I had just thought, “Okay, well, well, look, we did that, and let’s take the win.” Ken was there when we did that screening. It was brilliant, it was really good, but it’s not going to happen.

And then Spencer and Christian got in touch and said, “We formed this new label within Warner, and we’re doing The Devils director’s cut.” And, it was like, “Really?” Just like that. I spent a lot of time thinking, “What changed?” And I honestly think that what happened was: when The Devils came out, it caused such a furor, but also it got such a lot of flak for things that were just completely unfairly thrown at it. You know, “Oh, it’s disgusting, sensationalist, blasphemous, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.” And the cutting of the film—both by the censors and also by the studio at the time—sort of wounded Ken. He was really genuinely upset about it because he had taken the film very seriously. And we had sort of done a partial fix by getting the footage and showing that the film could be assembled in a version. The actual thing of it being restored properly to what it should have looked like is, even now, these months on from Cannes, I can’t quite believe it. So on the one hand: I’m immensely proud and I’m immensely happy that it’s happened; and on the other hand, there’s just a part of me that thinks, “Okay, how did we get…?”

The honest truth of it is: we got here because Spencer [Collantes] and Christian [Parkes] arrived at Warner Bros. and said, “We really want to do The Devils .” And because of the work that they had done at NEON… look, I am a 63-year-old man, right? Me obsessing about The Devils it’s like, “Yeah, well, I knew Ken. I promised Ken that we’d do this.” You know, “Okay, that’s fine, that’s just Mark being Mark, you know.” When Spencer and Christian—off the work thing, the success that they had at Neon—came to us and said, “We really want to do The Devils ,” I think that they went, “Oh, okay.” They’re smart. They’ve got their ear to the ground. They’ve got their finger on the pulse of what is happening now, which I don’t have; I’m an old man. And I think that that’s what changed, was that the kind of lack of enthusiasm for The Devils , which had really kind of dogged it throughout its history, was turned around by Spencer and Christian saying, “You know…” That’s a terrible phrase, but they’re young gunslingers and they come into town and go, “We think The Devils is really important.” And I think that they went, “Okay.”

From what I understand, and correct me if I’m wrong, but [WB] were nothing but supportive. And what it took was for them just to hear the right people say, “We think this is a really good idea.” And then, suddenly, it was a really good idea. Then there’s part of me that goes, “Oh, it was that simple.” It reminds me of the bit at the end of The Wizard of Oz when she says, “Yeah, you always had the ability to go home.” “The whole time?” Yeah. That’s what it took.

Mark Kermode and Lisi Tribble at the 64th New York Film Festival. Photo by Sean DiSerio.

Bit of a deus ex machina. Me being as a cinephile, you have your white whales, the movies that you never get to see or you never get to see in their purest form. Like, a lot of people are haunted by the thought of the longer Magnificent Ambersons , for instance, or like, last year I got to see one of my white whales, which is Patrick Tims’ Love Massacre , when it premiered at the Tokyo International Film Festival. And sometimes there’s that feeling where you finally see it and it’s not disappointing per se, but it is also a movie and a fixed runtime, and then it’s over, right? Which I think is maybe what partly what you’re getting at a little bit, that feeling of you can’t believe it and then suddenly it’s just happening.

Yeah, but I don’t feel like it’s just a movie and a runtime and then it’s over. I kind of feel like it’s out in the world finally. I mean, you’ve got to remember: I have thought about this for a really long time. I mean, not as long as Ken did, obviously

Sure.

For about a really, really long time. And every time, I mean… when I saw it in the Cannes premiere and it just looked astonishing. I mean, it just looked amazing. I hadn’t seen the restored version until it was in Cannes. And I was sitting there with Lisi [Tribble, Ken Russell’s widow] and we were both looking at each other going, “Did you know?” And I am really looking forward to tomorrow night. And somebody said to me, “You’re going to watch it again?” “Yes. Yes.” I’ve only seen it this good once. I now need to sit. I’d seen it 25, 30 times in the late-night circuit when I was watching the film and some old 35mm print in some butchered version. So, there’s no sense to me of, you know, “That’s it. It’s done now. It’s finished.” What I feel like is “That’s it. It’s done now. It’s beginning.” And what I really am excited to know is what happens now.

What will happen is that I will keep going back and seeing it every time. There’ll now be the release thing that would be great, and I will keep going back to see it because there is something about it as a complete film now that is the beginning of a story rather than the end of a story. And part of me thinks, what would it have been like if the film had been released like this in 1971?

Right.

Would people have understood it better? Would it have made more sense? I don’t, I don’t know. It was in one of the interviews I did earlier today, somebody said, “It’s like the film was waiting for the world to catch up with it.”

Definitely.

And I think the world hasn’t quite caught up with it yet. I think it’s closer than it was before. It was funny because of when Billy Friedkin did the re-cut of The Exorcist for “the version you’d never seen,” that I had written about the missing scenes, and the last sentence of the book that I wrote for the BFI about The Exorcist was —paraphrasing—we can only be tantalized by Bill Blatty’s suggestion that there was a better version of the film. And I took the line from—me being a hack—but I took the line from the publicity of the film: I said, “That thought is almost beyond comprehension” because the tagline for the film was, “Something almost beyond comprehension is happening to a girl in this house.” Dot, dot, dot—you know, dramatic flourish.

And then the stuff got put back in again. And that’s what I know about the closure thing: you go, “Oh, there we are.” There we are. And then people now said to me, “Well, is it better?” And the answer is, “No, it’s different.”

Okay.

“Okay, it’s different. It’s not better, it’s different.” In the case of The Devils , is it better? Yes. It is. It was damaged goods before. It had a big problem before because it was damaged. And now it isn’t damaged anymore. So, it’s not like in the case of The Exorcist —there wasn’t that sense of closure that you’re talking about. “Oh, okay, that’s it. That’s the thing that I was dreaming about.” In the case of this, I always knew that there was something wrong with it because the first time I ever spoke to Ken about it, he said to me, “It’s damaged goods.” That was the phrase that he used. He said, because they just took this stuff out of it, that left it with a hole. Something is damaged about it, and then you put it back in and go, “No, that is better. That is what it always should have looked like.”

Right.

And John Phillips—the theologian—said, fascinatingly, when he first saw the film, it was in Ken’s cut with the Rape of Christ sequence in it. And he said, “Despite the fact that that sequence was cut out, and it was never in the film from the release until now,” he said, in his mind, it was always there, because in his mind, it was part of the film. It was like, you know, it was.

I get it.

“But the rest of us had to wait to see what it was meant to look like.” So I kind of feel like now, after all this time, it’s finally being released for the first time. It’s like the things that people have seen of it up until now are sort of a trailer, but this is actually the film.

Sure.

Well, that’s so pretentious. I’m so sorry.

No, no, no, I think that’s great. I mean, because I think you’re speaking with enthusiasm. And I think sometimes enthusiasm and pretension get confused for each other. I want to circle back, because this is all on my mind, as you’re saying, “This is what the film should have looked like.” What was the DigiBeta of it?

So the DigiBeta that we had in 2000—in, whatever it was, 2000—when we were making Hell on Earth , we had found the missing scenes. We had found the reel of film that had the missing scenes on it, and we had digitized that. And we had put those scenes in Hell on Earth . So the first time the missing scenes were ever shown was on the Channel 4 documentary Hell on Earth , in which we had all those scenes in. The DigiBeta was a digital version of the British X-rated version, which had sort of disappeared from view, because the film opened in the UK with the British X rating. It was then further cut for the American version. So the American version was always shorter than the British version.

Okay, I see.

After the film had done its first run in cinemas, the British X-rated prints seemed to disappear and be superseded by the American R-rated prints. So for example: when I first saw the film, which was in either ’79 or ’80, either the winter of ’79 or… oh, the spring of ’80, the version that I saw, the version that was on the late-night circuit, was the American R-rated version. It had a British exit certificate at the beginning of it, but it wasn’t the British version; it was the American R-rated version. In fact, the British X-rated version was pretty much out of circulation until the late 1990s.

So we had the DigiBeta of the film in its most complete version, which was the British X-rated version. It was that version into which Mike Bradwell, who was the editor of both The Devils and of our documentary, re-inserted the two key sequences, which is the Rape of Christ sequence and the sequence with Sister Jeanne and the bone. But it was a digital video. So when we projected it onto screen one of the National Film Theater, it looked like a video projection. I mean, it was good, but it was a video.

Yes.

And the time that you noticed it the most was in those scenes when Grandier is addressing the crowd and the walls of Loudun, the white walls and the tiling inside. You know what Digi looks like?

I do. Terrible.

It goes a bit squiggly. And you were looking at it thinking, “It’s like watching it through a glass darkly. I can see that there… I can see that there is a brilliant thing there, but it’s.. it’s slightly obscured.” But what was fascinating was: at least you could see that that was what the film was meant to look like, but you had to kind of make the sort of leap of imagination as to what it would look like.

Yes.

When we finally saw the restoration, it was… I mean, Guillermo Del Toro has said this. It’s like, what was the comparison that he used? He said it was like cleaning the Sistine Chapel with saliva. And it was like, it was literally like, “Oh,” because: right. I quote this all the time, my friend Nigel Floyd, the film critic, says this thing the documentary Hell on Earth , and it’s my favorite comment about The Devils , and I repeat it all the time and people look at me like I’m being foolish. He said the thing about it is: it is a film which is a film. And what he meant by that is: it’s a film that is not a script. It is a film that is a film. It being a film quality was what it looked like.

Right.

And so up until the point of the restoration, it hadn’t actually looked like… so when it was first out in pristine print, fine, but the pristine prints were cut. And so therefore, there was something missing. Then when we finally restored it, fine, it had the rhythm, but it was from a DigiBeta. So finally, after all this time of imagining it, “Oh, that’s what it looks like.” And the Cannes thing was literally like we were just all sitting there going… I’ve imagined it, but it’s there. It’s better, or even better because you can’t quite describe—I can’t, because I’m not very good with words—you can’t quite describe in words what it does, because it is a film which is a film. Does that make any sense at all?

Behind the scenes of The Devils

Well, it’s funny. This resonates exactly with two things I was thinking while I was seeing the film. One is, like I said, sometimes when you encounter the white whale, it’s because it’s finally been restored. Other times, it’s a movie that you do know well, but you’ve only seen it on DVD or VHS, and when you see the restoration—I’ve had this thought multiple times—you literally didn’t know it could look like that.

Yeah, fine. You said it better.

Like, I thought it was embossed in amber as what the film looks like, and then… that’s insanely gratifying. But also the thing you say about “a film that looks like a film,” which is that I love all kinds of cinema, and I know that sometimes there’s a place for grandiosity, sometimes there’s a place for the homemade. But it kind of brought me back to this experience, with all that being said, of when I saw the final cut of Apocalypse Now at the Beacon Theater here in New York, which is a… I mean, it’s not even really a movie theater, that’s how big the screen is.

Okay.

And you’re sitting there and you’re watching it, and there’s something about a solidity of the image, on an image-by-image basis, of a certain force of detail, which, now I’m sounding pretentious. But there is something about that experience of: this is made in such a way, with such a density of image that goes beyond what we usually think of in film. I think especially as cinephiles, there’s this idea of sometimes you fetishize the thing that looks ugly or small, because that’s more dignified than something that’s big and grand.

Yeah, yeah, yeah.

But a movie like The Devils for me, those two streams cross.

Yes, I think that’s right. So the final cut of Apocalypse Now , does it have the plantation stuff in it? Does it have—

It does.

Fine. Okay.

And it was a great experience seeing it, because it was at the premiere, so nobody had seen it, and you could feel the air kind of suck out of the room when people realized it was going to stay in.

That’s interesting.

I kind of like that scene, and he also did a good job saying, like, “I like it too,” because he did a Q&A after. He was like, “I like it too, I want to keep it in.” But it was a funny experience.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. The interpolation thing is… I mean, the point you’re making about the sort of the deeper thing about looking at the image—you said it better than I did—the solidity of it, there’s something about Ken’s filmmaking when he is, and actually this kind of relates slightly to Apocalypse Now , it is very hard now to imagine a filmmaker being funded to make a film as out-there as The Devils was, because The Devils does not look like a film that anyone sat around and workshopped. Ken wrote the script for The Devils in a matter of weeks. He literally sat down and it came out of him, like he had the two books, he had the Whiting and he had the Huxley, and he just wrote. And then he had access to these sets and the sets were big, and it was a very, very big kind of ballroom set. And then he has access to the very finest acting talent—Oliver Reed, Vanessa Redgrave, Dudley Sutton, Michael Rainsford, and Georgina Hale. It’s extraordinary.

And then he has Peter Maxwell Davies doing the score, like literally the cutting-edge avant-garde composer of his stuff. All these things and then the costume by Shirley Russell, all these things together, it is hard to imagine a studio doing that again now. The only comparison I can think of is—recently, for example—Paul Thomas Anderson made One Battle After Another , and everyone was going, “It is astonishing that they allowed that amount of money to be spent on a movie that’s that adventurous.” And, okay, did well, but it’s a risk.

Sure.

In the case of The Devils , it’s like: the thing that is really remarkable about it is, it is a film that looked like, when he made it, was untrammeled. And then once he’d done it, they went, “No, no, no, sorry. No, no, no.” And then they had to start taking bits out of it, whereas now you’d think what would happen in advance is: you wouldn’t be able to make it in the first place. I don’t know. Maybe things are changing, because you hear people talking now about studios actually returning to a kind of auteur-driven thing, but it was a singular vision of a singular filmmaker who made films that were in a style that was very much his own, and he was allowed to do it, and then it was messed up after the fact.

Behind-the-scenes contiunity photos from The Devils.

I mean, there was applause in the end credits for Derek Jarman, too, from the audience, and it sort of begets the question: why isn’t every film set designed by someone of Jarman’s caliber?

Well, partly because not every filmmaker who’s making a a fairly decently budgeted studio movie would have the guts that Ken had, because the way that Ken got Derek Jarman—Ken told me this story—was he said that a friend of his had said, “I was on a train, I met this guy called Derek Jarman, he’s really interesting, I know you’re looking for a new look on The Devils , you should go see him.” So Ken goes, “Okay.” So Ken goes to Derek Jarman’s studio, which is on the banks of the Thames, and it’s this great big warehouse, and he walks in and it’s freezing cold, and in the middle of it, there is a greenhouse with Derek Jarman sitting in it with a two-bar electric fire, and all the way around the walls are this exhibition of his see-through Cardinal’s coats, and one of them’s filled with dollars, and one of them’s filled with stuff that he found washed up in the Thames, and one of them’s, you know…

And Ken looks at these things, and he goes, “This guy’s got ideas,” and he sits, and he talks to Derek Jarman for hours, and he just goes, “Yep, him. Him. Come and design this massive studio production that we’re making at Pinewood Studios, in which we’re literally going to build Loudun. Do that.” That is the risk. It’s like, not only did Ken take the risk—he was able to take the risk. He was able to go, “Yeah, I’m going to make this movie with this guy. You haven’t heard of him, but I think he’s a genius.” I was talking to somebody earlier on, saying there is an argument for saying that The Devils is Derek Jarman’s first feature, right? Because it is a Derek Jarman movie in the same way that it’s a Ken Russell movie. And it’s funny now that everybody celebrates the thing about, “You know, it’s Derek Jarman,” and his name comes across the screen every because, of course, it’s Derek Jarman, but at the time, nobody knew who Derek Jarman was—he was just Ken thought, “No, he’s brilliant, he’ll do it.”

Yeah, if it was very similar to it in minimalist, people would see Derek Jarman at the end and go, “Oh. Oh, strange, okay.” A few things to branch off from there, but I watched this video of you and Russell doing a Q&A about the film probably 20 or so years ago, and towards the end there’s an interesting conversation you guys had about the concept of kitsch.

Yeah.

And he said, which I think is a good quote, “Kitsch is fine.” And you’re also talking about the film coming out now and you’re wondering how the response is going to be. This not just advocate, but this kind of shepherd for the film, do you feel confident about how a fresh audience is going to respond to it? Or is confidence not even part of it? Is concern not part of it? It goes into the world and people respond how they do?

Well, I’ll be honest with you: I am incredibly bullheaded. Right? I have always thought it was a masterpiece, sure. And I have never understood anyone not thinking that. Ken and I bonded when I first met him because it’s quite easy to bond with somebody who tells you that the film that you’ve made that caused you no manner of trouble, just goes, “No, I think it’s a work of genius and I think you’re a genius and I think it’s a masterpiece and I think we have to put it back together again and fix it.” There is no part of me that doubts for one minute that the film is a masterpiece. I have been very aware of the fact that it was a wrongly maligned masterpiece, of which there have been many over the history of cinema. I’ve never, ever doubted that it was anything other than a masterpiece. The real delight has been this sort of growing groundswell of other voices saying the same thing.

So some time ago, Sight and Sound did one of those polls of everyone’s favorite movies. There were only two people then who put The Devils in their top 10. It was me, and the other one was Alex Cox. And that was 20, however many years ago it was. And then over the years, other voices start to join in, and then when we did the restoration, at the end people were very interested and then Guillermo [Del Toro] is talking about his love for Ken Russell—as a longstanding love for Ken Russell. So okay, there’s a rising tide of voices that the film is much better than perhaps its initial review. So by the time we get to this point, it’s like I’m thinking, “Everyone who knows anything knows that the film is a masterpiece. And if you don’t think it’s a masterpiece, you’re wrong.”

Sure.

But when we got to Cannes, there is the moment just before the film starts, and then it comes on the screen, and literally it comes on the screen with the theatrical production of the Venus thing, and you can hear people going, “Sorry, which film is this? The opening… is this how The Devils opens?” Because people think of the play; they don’t think of that. And so after that Cannes screening, the response was so rapturous, it was just like, “Oh, well, there we go. Of course. There we are. That’s it.” But there’s no part of me that feels any nervousness about how it will… I’m sure that there will be some people who will react negatively to it, some people will react positively to it, as is always the case with any movie at all. But I have no doubt that it is a film that will command serious attention and will be taken seriously, as it always should have been.

But that’s partly because I am very pigheaded, and I have believed that since I first saw it. I mean, there was a lot of bad stuff written about The Devils . Reviews when it first came out accused it of all manner of terrible things. And you read the BBFC reports, they thought it was disgraceful and disgusting, and you go, “No, it isn’t. It is a work of art.” And so yeah, no: I don’t feel any anxiety or worry about it at all. I was delighted by how it played in Cannes, but I kind of think like the world has caught up with it and that, if I’m really honest with you, the way that I feel right now is smug. “See? They flew you across the ocean to be here.”

You should be. You know, anytime I get put on a paid flight, I’m feeling so smug. And I’m not getting the honors.

But it is just that kind of thing. It’s just like, “See? There’s the evidence, right?” Because there were times when I was at Time Out in the 1980s, one of my editors said to me once, “Your problem is that you don’t believe that there is such a… you think…” No, the exact phrase was, said, “Your problem is that you believe that all art is redeemable.” And I said, “What do you—what do you even mean by that?” And they said, “Well, you just, you believe things.” And they were speaking, as it happened, about a conversation we had about Caligula , right? Because I had said somewhere in the middle of the car crash of a movie that is Caligula , there is a half-decent film struggling to get out. Well, I don’t know whether you saw the Caligula recut from a couple of years ago.

I did not.

It’s really good. And I did an interview with Malcolm McDowell, because over the years I had been involved in sort of various [ways]. Now, Caligula is never going to be a masterpiece. I’m not comparing The Devils to Caligula , but there was something in there, which was really Malcolm McDowell’s performance. And I had interviewed Malcolm McDowell, and he had talked about the heartbreak of it, that he had given this performance, and then it had turned into Caligula —this spectacular car crash of a film. And then when this new recut finally got done—it was a couple of years ago; two, three years ago—he said for the first time ever, he was able to go, “ See ? That’s what I thought we were doing.”

Yeah.

And so there’s part of me that just thinks when you—having said for such a long time that The Devils is a masterpiece—I never said Caligula was a masterpiece. Having said for a long time that The Devils is a masterpiece—it is Ken Russell’s best film, it is Ken Russell’s most underrated and misunderstood film—and now I literally feel like going, “ See ?” Sorry. When you transcribe this, it will just be Mark saying “ See ” over and over again.

I think the emphasis on it will be good. I mean, it’s funny because you met Russell in the mid-90s, which means you probably knew him for the last 15 or so years of his life. There’s an interesting question about the filmmaker-critic relationship. I think it’s interesting because you are very renowned as a critic, but you also have historian, advocate—there are a few hats that I think you wear. And how does your relationship with a director’s filmography change when you form your relationship with the director? It’s not like you necessarily love or even like every film that they’ve made, but are you looking at their films through a particular, different lens once you know them as a person?

So when I met Ken in 1995, his feature-film career had pretty much finished. At that point, he was what he referred to as a “garagist” because he made films in his garage. And he made independent films that were, like, absolutely independently funded because he couldn’t get money to make features. He didn’t have ideas—he did, but the British film industry was not very kind to Ken in his later years. So by the time I met him, the body of work existed substantially in terms of his feature films. And I knew what I thought about those films, because I had seen The Devils and Tommy and Women in Love and Music Lovers and Marlor and The Devils and Crimes of Passion and I had seen all the films, and I knew what I thought about them.

So it wasn’t like I was going to meet Ken and it was going to radically change the way I thought about the films, because I already kind of knew how I did think about them. The other thing was that, despite the fact that I knew Ken pretty well over the 15 years, I never stopped being a fan. I couldn’t quite believe that we were going round to Ken’s house. I couldn’t quite believe that I was on first-name terms with Ken. I mean, it was like literally for 15, 16 years, I had to keep pinching myself and going, “It’s Ken Russell in my kitchen.” You know, “We’re going to the pub with Ken Russell. I’m doing an onstage with Ken Russell.”

Absolutely.

And although people find it quite hard to believe, the same was true of Billy Friedkin. I never, ever got over the fact that Billy, he gave me a copy of, I think, the Cruising soundtrack, and he wrote a thing in it, which said, you know, “Thanks for all your support over the years, and your friendship.”

And I was like, “Are we friends?” You know, but because the imbalance was never going away. It was never going because he was—he was Billy Friedkin. He made The Exorcist and Sorcerer and films that were really, really good. Now, that didn’t mean that I loved everything he did. I didn’t. There were plenty of films that he made that weren’t to my liking. I didn’t like The Guardian one bit. I didn’t like Deal of the Century , an absolute mess of a film. Total mess of a film. I mean, it’s a weird thing, because Billy always said, “Yeah, it was a great script,” but it… and you think, “Really?” But so he made plenty of films that I didn’t like. It didn’t matter. It didn’t in any way affect what I thought about him as a filmmaker, and it didn’t affect what he thought about me, because it wasn’t like he didn’t know, because the stuff was all published. So there were some films of his that I really liked that he couldn’t quite understand why I really liked them.

Right.

So in the case of Ken, there are things that Ken did that, I think that we know, are more important than some other things that he did. But when you look at some of the later work, like Lair of the White Worm is now a film that people really love as a cult movie.

The Devils

It shows up on streaming every October for horror programming.

And I bet people watch it and go, “Wow, you ever seen Lair of the White Worm ?” And that was a film which, when it first came out, people didn’t think, “Oh, that’s a film that’s going to last, however many years it’s been.” But now it is an absolute die-hard cult classic. And I think that probably when I first met Ken and we talked about his movies, that wasn’t one of the movies that I talked to him about, because I was talking to him about Women in Love and The Devils and all the rest of it.

I see.

But even when, after all those years we had known each other, I was still a Ken Russell fanboy. So I don’t think it fundamentally changed anything because if somebody is a great filmmaker and they make a bad film, it doesn’t make them a bad filmmaker.

Sure.

And one of the things that people say is like, “Well, if you like a filmmaker, then you are much more inclined to be kind to their work.” To which the answer is: “Yeah. That’s how it works.” If you think that somebody is an admirable filmmaker and they make a bad film, it’s more interesting than if somebody who isn’t an admirable filmmaker makes a bad film because people’s failures are kind of interesting. If you believe that the intent, the intention, the artistic ambition is worthy, that does affect how you think about films. So yes: when people say, “Well, you tend to be kinder to the films of directors that you like,” yeah, but it’s not I like them personally. I got to know them because I like their work.

And that’s the case with both Billy Friedkin and with Ken Russell: I got to know them because I was obsessed with their work, and I wrote about their work, and then I was privileged to meet them and make documentaries about them. As a result of that, we had a relationship that, on one level, you could define as a friendship, but on another level—and Ken, God bless him, was really good about this. He knew that if he was going to spend an evening with Mark, half of that evening was going to be taken up with Mark going, “Now, Ken, tell me: when you did Women in Love , what lenses were you using with that?” That requires a certain amount of patience, because as anybody who is a great artist knows, you don’t necessarily want to be surrounded by your greatest fan. It must get quite annoying.

Chris Farley and Paul McCartney.

Yeah.

Yeah, I’ve caught myself doing it too.

Yeah, and it’s really hard not to. Because it’s Ken Russell and you’re just having a nice time, and then you go, “Okay, you know that scene in Altered States …”

What you’re saying about the “fundamentally more interesting”—I mean, that’s point origin for a concept of auteurism, as Truffaut wrote about it before he ever shot a frame of film. He said, a bad film by a great filmmaker is more interesting than any… and I think you still see people blanch at that a little bit, and I think it’s interesting because it gets into this level of… it’s not about biases necessarily, or lowering your critical faculties, but I think it’s this strange median point between critical faculties and a sort of unbridled enthusiasm. It’s this weird place where they meet.

Yeah. But I honestly think that one of the things I find very hard is the idea of objective criticism. Criticism is not objective, right? It is personal. Now, there are things about it that are objective: being factually correct about a movie. Like, one of the things that Ken was so incensed about Alex Walker’s review of The Devils in the Evening Standard —and you know the famous story that Alex Walker really didn’t like the film—Ken was incensed because there were two things that Alex Walker said in the review that did not happen in the film. One of them was that we see Grandier’s penis being crushed. We don’t. It doesn’t happen; it doesn’t happen. So they were on a late-night BBC talk show and Ken said to Alex Walker, “You’ve said these things in this review and they’re not true.” Alex wasn’t having any of it. So Ken lost his temper and he got up and he smacked Alex Walker over the head with his own review of the film and walked off. This was then a kind of a subject of great, great scandal—of course it was. But the thing that outraged him wasn’t that Alex Walker didn’t like the film; it’s that he said things about it that weren’t true.

Sure. Of course.

And so there are things that are objectively true, right? Who directed the film? Who wrote the film? How did the film get made? Then there are things which are objectively true about placing it within the context and the industry of other versions—is it a remake? Is it a novel adaptation? Where does it sit? There are other things which are objectively true about it, which is: it is this long, or it is this long, it was cut, or it wasn’t. These are objective, actual truths. Beyond that, how you respond to it is nothing but personal. And I find it very… the older I get—and I am very old—the more I think that the only way of being honest about it is to be honest about how personal it is.

I agree .

There was always something that was very difficult about writing for the Monthly Film Bulletin —that they said, “You need to write objectively.” And I tried really hard, but it was like: it was a lie. Me writing objectively was me trying to pretend that something that I thought was objectively true—it’s not objectively true, it’s subjectively true. This is how I respond to the film. And that is what all film criticism is. That’s why opinions differ about things, because everything is subjective. There are things that are objectively, factually correct, true, and then there are things which are your opinions. And the only way you can do that honestly is to be honest about how personal they are, because films are a very personal thing.

One of the reasons that film censorship is quite complicated is because it works on a principle that you can predict how people react to material, broadly speaking, and you can’t. People react strangely to different things, particularly to a sin, to a medium as kind of as vibrant as cinema. This is a very long way of saying that in the end, for me, it’s all personal. It’s all to do with: I attach my affections to films that touch me in a certain way, and I hope that I describe them in a way that makes that make sense, even if you don’t agree with a single word of it. So you can go, “Okay, well, Kermode likes it. But then, of course Kermode likes it.” And even when that comes down to “Kermode,” I said, “Well, of course he likes it, because he likes Ken Russell.” That in itself is a valid criticism, because yes: I do like Ken Russell, and if you understand that I like Ken Russell, that is partly an explanation of why it is that I like the film, because I like the artistic swing, I like the… I like the intent.

And some films are made with more of what I would consider to be valid intent, and some films, there’s no part of me that thinks that when Michael Bay was making the Transformers movies, that he was inspired by a desire to tell those stories in the best possible, life-changing way. I don’t know, because I never met the guy.

Sure.

But when I look at them, they just look like bank balances. They just look like a bunch of numbers.

Mark Kermode and Lisi Tribble at the 64th New York Film Festival. Photo by Sean DiSerio.

Yeah. I mean, I think that’s a perfectly valid way of summarizing what’s a very difficult concept that seems like it’s always swimming around. As a way of closing the circle on this—this dream has been fulfilled, and it’s been fulfilled in a way that I think is beyond anybody’s, like I said, six months ago I wouldn’t have thought I’d be sitting there watching a 35mm print to this in its version. With that in mind, what, if anything, is second on the list of “White Whale, I want to see it.”

Well, I don’t know.

I also understand if there’s a hundred things tied for second place.

There almost isn’t. It’s partly an age thing. It’s partly what you refer to as my “white whales” have sailed. I saw The Exorcist and The Devils together on a late-night double bill in 1979. I saw them both on the same evening, right? That is probably the formative experience of my cinema-going life: those two films, one after the other. And then I have obsessed about those two films henceforth. Those two films now exist in the versions—as you said, The Exorcist exists in two versions. One of them is different to the other one. The Devils now exists in the version that it should have existed in. There isn’t anything else that’s burning up, and also because there isn’t anything else that has obsessed me that much over the years. [Note: after our interview, Mark would note that his white whale would be a remastered director’s cut of William Peter Blatty’s The Exorcist III .]

So I’m kind of probably done. I mean, I’m 63. I’m not going to discover another thing now that I’ve got to, that I’m going to be obsessed about for 30 years. So no: I’m probably, in terms of those things, I’m done, and that’s fine. I’m just very, very pleased that this came about and we got to see it. My only regret is I wish Ken had been here to see it, and I do, but I do think that when the film is projected in an auditorium with an audience, he sort of is, sure. And I do believe that. I do think that there is something transcendent about that experience. But I wish he’d been there; I wish he’d been able to be there so that we could all go, “ See ?”

I do. I’ve seen this film, I want to spend more time with the films of Ken Russell, which I haven’t spent as much time with as, admittedly, I should. And so it’s like that saying: You die twice—the first time is your body, the second time is the last time somebody says your name.

Oh, I didn’t know that. Wow.

Yeah, that’s an old saying. And how many times is Ken Russell’s name being said today and tomorrow night?

Well, I do think it’s the start of something. I do genuinely think it’s the start of something. I think it’s like this is the birth of The Devils , and if it leads people back to the back catalog—I mean, there’s so much to discover. There is so many great films in there. And there are films that you’ll love, and films that you’ll hate, and films that you’ll be baffled by, and films that you’ll be dazzled by, and films that you will come out afterwards and go to the pub and have really heated discussions about what was going on.

I mean, I love Altered States . I absolutely love Altered States . The first time I saw Altered States was in the Empire Leicester Square in the West End of London, and I absolutely love every minute of it. And then I read some reviews of it, like, “Did we see the same film?” No. It was just, like, I couldn’t—I couldn’t quite understand, and then as I said, everything is personal, everything is. You like Altered States ? It’s a great film. The human spirit, the whole thing about the tangible encounter and “I’m going to find the fucker.” Ken and Lisi once did this thing which—they had lines from Ken’s film on ticker tape, and they would give them to people as a gift, and they gave me “And I’m going to find the fucker.”

And in a way, you have found the fucker.

And, well, I have found the fucker—yeah.

Uncut and restored, The Devils opens in theaters on Friday, October 16.

title_original: «Dove dobbiamo andare, se la nostra casa è già qui?» Se lo chiede ‘Cittadini!’ di Dora García, a Verona
editorial_title_zh: «我们若已在此处，又该去往何方？»——多拉·加西亚维 Verona 展出的《公民们！》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在福蒂宫的庭院里，多拉·加西亚上演了一场参与式行为艺术，借用政治游行的语言，质问公民身份的意义、第二代移民的权利以及社会中的排他形式……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "福蒂宫庭院的柱廊下，一群年轻人站立着，面对着另一群人。这一场景让人想起学生游行或政治抗议活动。参与者脚边放着标语牌，他们很可能会在不久后举起这些牌子；他们开始交谈。粗砺的嗓音交替重叠，最终汇成一种集体演讲，时而如同合唱，时而宛如独白。这就是多拉·加西亚（Dora García）的行为艺术《公民们！》（Cittadini!），该作品由她与玛琳·范托尼（Marlene Fantoni）合作创作、劳拉·拉莫内亚（Laura Lamonea）策展，作为第21届维罗纳艺博会（ArtVerona）的一部分在维罗纳呈现。这一干预创作探讨了公民身份与包容的主题，将福蒂宫的历史与当下政治和社会辩论中的议题联系起来。地点的选择是该项目不可或缺的一部分。庭院内设有先贤祠（Famedio），保存着在意大利殖民战争和第一次世界大战中阵亡的维罗纳人的名字。行为艺术将这座纪念性记忆场所与当前关于权利、民族认同以及具移民背景人士（特别是第二代移民）处境的讨论联系在了一起。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/ArtVerona_2026_Veronafiere_EnneviFoto_FNT57932-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Dora García, Cittadini!, Palazzo Forti, Verona. Ph. Ennevi Foto", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对该建筑历史的引用还涉及阿基莱·福蒂（Achille Forti）的人物形象，他于1937年将这座宫殿及其个人收藏捐赠给维罗纳市。1938年种族法的颁布，在一年后为机构、归属感和权利之间的关系引入了一个显著的矛盾。从这些历史层积出发，加西亚构建了一项面向当下的干预创作，特别关注鼓吹排外的政治立场以及所谓的“再移民”议题。作为一位生活和工作在巴塞罗那与奥斯陆之间的西班牙艺术家，多拉·加西亚长期以来一直致力于以社会关系的政治维度、参与形式以及社群角色为核心的研究。行为艺术是她实践的主要工具之一，往往让公众参与其中，并对作品的创作者、参与者和旁观者之间的界限提出质疑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/ArtVerona_2026_Veronafiere_EnneviFoto_FNT57934-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Dora García, Cittadini!, Palazzo Forti, Verona. Ph. Ennevi Foto", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在多拉·加西亚的《公民们！》中，这种构思转化为了一场集体行动，通过与移民背景的本地社群实体以及维罗纳美术学院（Accademia di Belle Arti di Verona）的学生的合作共同构建。参与者直接面向公众朗读文本，并使用共同制作的标语牌，呼用了政治示威的传达方式。其结果是一种唤起抗议语言却又不同于传统游行或动员的场景：抗议的形式成了一种机制，借此讨论谁可以被认可以及在什么条件下被认可为公民。公众发现自己身处一个不仅要求跟随行动、更邀请反思自身在所涉主题中立场的境地中。这些人重申了被认可为社群一部分的可能性，突显出公民身份不仅关乎法律地位，还关乎社会划定自身边界并决定谁能成为其中一员的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "多拉·加西亚的这一干预创作纳入了“第二时光 | 福蒂宫”（Secondo Tempo | Palazzo Forti）项目，该项目由维罗纳市政府、市民博物馆——阿基莱·福蒂现代艺术画廊（Galleria d’Arte Moderna Achille Forti）以及卡里维罗纳基金会（Fondazione Cariverona）共同发起，并得到了西班牙文化行动署（Acción Cultural Española, AC/E）的支持。该项目伴随着福蒂宫的重新开放与活化进程，这座宫殿于2025年重新对公众开放，通过将当代艺术、历史遗产与城市语境相对话的文化项目推进。", "links": [{"text": "Galleria d ’ Arte Moderna Achille Forti", "url": "https://gam.comune.verona.it/nqcontent.cfm?a_id=43329"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Una folla di giovani, sotto il portico del cortile di Palazzo Forti, è disposta in piedi di fronte a un altro gruppo di persone. La scena ricorda quella di una manifestazione studentesca o di un presidio politico. I partecipanti hanno sotto ai loro piedi dei cartelli, che probabilmente innalzeranno poco dopo; iniziano a parlare. Le voci grosse si alternano e si sovrappongono, fino a diventare un discorso collettivo, a tratti corale, a tratti monologico. È Cittadini! , la performance di Dora Garc í a , realizzata in collaborazione con Marlene Fantoni e a cura di Laura Lamonea, presentata a Verona nell ’ ambito della ventunesima edizione di ArtVerona. L ’ intervento affronta il tema della cittadinanza e dell ’ inclusione, mettendo in relazione la storia di Palazzo Forti con le questioni che attraversano oggi il dibattito politico e sociale. La scelta del luogo è parte integrante del progetto. Nel cortile si trova infatti il Famedio, che conserva i nomi dei veronesi caduti nelle guerre coloniali italiane e durante la Prima Guerra Mondiale. Un monumento alla memoria che la performance mette in relazione con le attuali discussioni sui diritti, sull ’ identit à nazionale e sulla condizione delle persone con background migratorio, in particolare delle seconde generazioni.

Il riferimento alla storia dell ’ edificio riguarda anche la figura di Achille Forti, che nel 1937 don ò il palazzo e la propria collezione alla citt à di Verona. La promulgazione delle leggi razziali nel 1938 introdusse, a un anno di distanza, una contraddizione significativa nel rapporto tra istituzioni, appartenenza e diritti. A partire da queste stratificazioni storiche Garc í a costruisce un intervento rivolto al presente, con particolare attenzione alle posizioni politiche che promuovono l ’ esclusione e al tema della cosiddetta « remigrazione » . Artista spagnola che vive e lavora tra Barcellona e Oslo, Dora Garc í a sviluppa da tempo una ricerca incentrata sulla dimensione politica delle relazioni sociali, sulle forme di partecipazione e sul ruolo delle comunit à . La performance è uno degli strumenti principali della sua pratica, che spesso coinvolge il pubblico e mette in discussione la distinzione tra chi realizza un ’ opera, chi vi prende parte e chi la osserva.

In Cittadini! di Dora García questa impostazione si traduce in un ’ azione collettiva costruita attraverso la collaborazione con realt à associative del territorio legate ai contesti migratori e con gli studenti dell ’ Accademia di Belle Arti di Verona. I partecipanti recitano testi rivolgendosi direttamente al pubblico e utilizzano cartelli realizzati collettivamente, riprendendo le modalit à comunicative delle manifestazioni politiche. Il risultato è una situazione che richiama il linguaggio della protesta senza coincidere con un corteo o con una mobilitazione tradizionale: la forma della manifestazione diventa il dispositivo attraverso cui discutere chi possa essere riconosciuto come cittadino e a quali condizioni. Il pubblico si trova destinatario di una situazione che non richiede soltanto di seguire l’azione, ma invita a interrogarsi sulla propria posizione rispetto ai temi affrontati. Sono persone che rivendicano la possibilit à di essere riconosciute come parte della comunit à , mettendo in evidenza come la cittadinanza non riguardi soltanto uno status giuridico, ma anche le modalit à attraverso cui una societ à definisce i propri confini e decide chi pu ò farne parte.

L ’ intervento di Dora García si inserisce nel programma Secondo Tempo | Palazzo Forti, promosso dal Comune di Verona, dai Musei Civici – Galleria d ’ Arte Moderna Achille Forti e da Fondazione Cariverona, e realizzato con il sostegno di Acci ó n Cultural Espa ñ ola (AC/E). Il progetto accompagna il percorso di riapertura e valorizzazione di Palazzo Forti, tornato accessibile al pubblico nel 2025, attraverso una programmazione culturale che mette in dialogo arte contemporanea, patrimonio storico e contesto cittadino.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "上周，德维卡（Devika）从东京国际电影节归来，该电影节于10月27日至11月5日在日本首都举行。作为亚洲的主要电影节之一，该活动是展示该地区新片与修复影片以及日本特有动画等门类的重要窗口。在此期间，德维卡录制了三期播客，与一众杰出的嘉宾共同探讨了电影节的片单。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "首先，影评人瓦迪姆·里佐夫（Vadim Rizov）和孔·里蒂（Kong Rithdee）加盟，共同讨论了一些重磅竞赛片，包括最终斩获最佳影片大奖的安娜玛丽·雅西尔（Annemarie Jacir）的《巴勒斯坦36》（Palestine 36），以及潘礼德（Rithy Panh）的纪录片《我们是森林的果实》（We Are the Fruits of the Forest）；此外还有保罗·施拉德（Paul Schrader）的《三岛由纪夫传》（Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters）在拍摄完成40年后，终于迎来了日本官方迟到的首映。接着，影评人坎博尔·坎贝尔（Kambole Campbell）和萨莎·韩（Sasha Han）分别从各自的专业领域——动画和东南亚电影——讨论了入选影片。其中的亮点包括二战宣传片兼日本历史上第一部动画长片《桃太郎 海之神兵》（Momotaro, Sacred Sailors）；押井守的邪典经典《天使之卵》（Angel’s Egg）；以及彭力·云旦拿域安的美食惊悚片《Morte Cucina》。最后，策展人、翻译兼制片人增渕爱子（Aiko Masubuchi）分享了她对三部日本电影的看法。第一部是1985年的纪录片《山：攻击与攻击》（Yama: Attack to Attack），在电影节场外放映；后两部《失落之地》（Lost Land）和《在他们的足迹中》（In Their Traces）则是其“日本现今电影”（Nippon Cinema Now）单元的亮点。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Last week, Devika returned from the Tokyo International Film Festival, which ran from October 27 to November 5 in the Japanese capital. As one of the major festivals in Asia, the event is a great showcase for new and restored films from the region, as well as Japanese specialities like animation. While there, Devika recorded three Podcasts exploring the lineup with a stellar rotation of guests.

First up, critics Vadim Rizov and Kong Rithdee join to talk about some of the big competition titles, including Annemarie Jacir’s Palestine 36 , which ended up winning the Grand Prix, and Rithy Panh’s documentary We Are the Fruits of the Forest ; as well as the the long-overdue official Japanese premiere of Paul Schrader’s Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters , 40 years after its making. Next, critics Kambole Campbell and Sasha Han discuss selections from their areas of expertise—respectively, animation and Southeast Asian cinema. Some highlights include Momotaro, Sacred Sailors , a piece of WWII propaganda and the first-ever animated feature made in Japan; Mamoru Oshii’s cult classic Angel’s Egg ; and Pen-ek Ratanaruang’s culinary thriller Morte Cucina. Finally, programmer, translator, and producer Aiko Masubuchi shares her thoughts on three Japanese titles. The first, Yama: Attack to Attack , a documentary from 1985, was screened outside of the festival; the latter two, Lost Land and In Their Traces , were highlights of its Nippon Cinema Now section.
excerpt_original: Taking the stage: a stellar rotation of critics explore the lineup of one of Asia’s major film events
